I always thought B2C marketing had a more interesting story to tell, but it turns out I was wrong. 

As someone interested in the overlap of psychology and marketing, I always found B2C to be more interesting, creative, and relatable. B2B, for one reason or another, seemed a little less exciting. As Chris Willman put it, we often think of B2B as B2C's "duller younger sibling." 

My perception completely changed yesterday during our guest lecture with Chris, a marketing strategist and Fractional CMO who has spent over 20 years working with global technology and cybersecurity companies.

One takeaway was the differences in the psychology behind the buying process. While B2C often involves individual purchasing decisions influenced by emotion, convenience, and brand, B2B involves multiple stakeholders, various touch points, and a much longer decision-making cycle. The most interesting distinction was that buying behavior is impacted by trust, ROI, and risk, rather than driven by impulse, emotional desire, and aspirations around identity.

Chris also explained how AI is reshaping the B2B landscape. He mentioned that by the time a potential client reaches you, they've already (almost) decided what their decision is based on evidence you didn't see. Chris explained that 49% of B2B buyers use AI-powered research tools to evaluate vendors, and 67% have no interest in speaking with a salesperson. 

Marketing seems to no longer be about reaching the right audience, so how can businesses start to build trust far before the conversation begins?

Thank you Chris Willman for providing such an insightful session!

Most times, when customers delay buying from you… it’s not because they don’t want your product.⁣

It’s mostly not even because of the price.⁣

A lot of the time, there is a psychology behind it, it's mostly not about the discount on the product... (Let me explain)⁣

There are 4 major emotional reasons people delay buying, and if you understand these, you’ll stop losing customers who actually want to buy from you especially this Black Friday season 

Let’s briefly talk about them…⁣⁣⁣⁣⁣

1️⃣. They are scared of making the wrong decision:⁣⁣
Nobody wants to buy something and regret it.⁣⁣
⁣
Nobody wants to look back at something and say, "I just wasted my money on this; it did not work for me."⁣
⁣
You don’t know how many people want what you're selling… but they hold themselves back thinking:⁣
⁣
What if this doesn’t work for me?⁣
⁣
What if I waste my money again?⁣
⁣
What if I regret it?⁣
⁣
This fear alone stops more sales than your price ever will.⁣
⁣
People buy faster when they feel safe.⁣
⁣
2️⃣. They feel overwhelmed.⁣⁣
⁣
Sometimes your offer is good… but it’s doing too much.⁣
⁣
Too many features. Too many decisions. Too many options.⁣
⁣
When a customer feels overwhelmed, the brain responds with one default reaction:⁣
⁣
“I’ll come back later.”⁣
⁣
And you already know what “later” means most time… right?⁣
⁣
Later = they forget. 
Later = they move on. 
Later = Mostly lost forever.⁣
⁣
You should make buying from you simple and easy.⁣
⁣⁣
3️⃣. They see no urgency.⁣
⁣
If your customer feels like nothing changes whether they buy now or next month…⁣⁣ They will delay.⁣
⁣
People move fast when there is something to gain now or something to lose later.⁣
⁣
Urgency is not about putting fake timers.⁣
⁣
It is showing them what disappears if they wait:⁣
⁣
– A bonus⁣
– A discount⁣
– A slot⁣
⁣
Make buying later cost them something.⁣
⁣
Make buying now, reward them.⁣⁣
⁣
4️⃣. They don’t feel emotionally connected to your message.⁣
⁣
People buy emotionally first, logically second.⁣
⁣
If your message feels too stiff, too technical, too feature-heavy…⁣
⁣
You won’t move them (your customers).⁣
⁣
A customer buys immediately when she feels understood, seen, and safe.⁣
⁣
When she feels like,⁣ ...this person gets me… this is exactly what I need...⁣
⁣
You don't need to sound smart, just make them feel something.⁣
⁣
Make them see themselves in a better place after buying from you.⁣
⁣
At the end of the day, people don’t delay because they don’t want the product.⁣
⁣
If you understand and handle these 4 emotional reasons, you’ll stop losing customers who actually want to buy from you.⁣
⁣
This will help you sell a lot of Volume this Black Friday.

If your sales team routinely relies on discounts to close deals, you don't have a pricing problem.

You have an emotional endurance problem.

In strategy rooms across mid-market and SME businesses, founders often tell me: 
"The market has become brutal. Buyers only care about price."

Yet, when we audit live sales interactions, a completely different pattern appears.

The concession rarely comes from an aggressive buyer. 
It is surrendered by the salesperson—often before the client has even asked for it.

Here is the behavioral breakdown happening on your sales floor:

1. The Resistance Trap
When a qualified prospect says, "Your competitor is 20% cheaper," it is rarely a final decision. It is an instinctive friction test. The prospect is assessing whether your team genuinely believes in the ROI they just presented.

2. Silence Intolerance
An untrained rep experiences buyer hesitation as rejection. The human brain naturally rushes to resolve psychological tension. In high-stakes sales, panic almost always speaks the language of premature price drops.

3. Scripting vs. Regulation
This is precisely where conventional corporate training collapses. 
Companies continuously invest in teaching product features and rigid pitch scripts. But a script is useless the moment a prospective client deviates from the manual. 

Real capability is not memorizing what to say. 
Real capability is nervous-system regulation under commercial pressure.

If your professionals cannot comfortably navigate an uncomfortable objection without flinching, no pricing model or marketing campaign will protect your margins.

Execution discipline in sales isn't about closing louder. 
It is about building teams with the conversational stamina to defend value when the room gets quiet.

Before you adjust your targets or alter your pricing strategy this quarter, look closely at the conversations taking place:

Are your people genuinely losing to the market, or are they negotiating against themselves?

Here's yesterday's "Wednesday Moment Of Wisdom", which I forgot to share. 🤦‍♂️ 


Wednesday’s Moment of Wisdom:
Disqualifying a lead > Qualifying 


Not every prospect should become an opportunity.
Sometimes the best outcome of a discovery conversation is realizing there isn’t enough pain or urgency to justify moving forward.
Three simple questions can help.

Ask about their current state/solution.
1: "What are you using now?" -Or- "How are you handling this today"

This isn’t the time to jump into priorities, goals, or your solution. Just understand their current state.
Listen closely. Their answer will usually reveal whether they have:

-An existing process
-A competitor
-Nothing in place at all


Then go one level deeper with your second question. 
2: "What's broken about it?" -Or- “What’s not working?”
Notice the wording. You're not asking IF something is broken. Ask WHAT is broken. 

If the answer is, “Nothing really,” pay attention.

There may be no meaningful problem to solve right now. 
Disqualify them and move on.

That doesn’t mean forget about them. No pain today doesn’t mean no pain tomorrow. Stay connected, but don’t manufacture an opportunity that doesn’t exist.


Finally ask them what happens if it stays broken. 
3: “If this continues for another six months or a year, what does that cost you?”

If they can’t identify an impact, there may not be enough urgency to act.

But, if they can put a number, consequence, or business impact around it, even a rough one, they’ve just qualified themselves. 

Pain gives someone a reason to change. Urgency gives them a reason to change NOW!


As sales professionals, our job isn’t to convince every prospect that they have a problem.
It’s to ask great questions that help them determine whether the problem is important enough to solve.

And sometimes, the smartest sales move is knowing when to walk away.

The Scenario: Your sales team is having productive conversations. Buyers are engaged, relationships are developing, and there's genuine interest in moving forward. The Play: Teach reps to recognize when a buyer's decision-making environment is becoming more complicated. Instead of increasing the pressure to move forward, help the buyer regain clarity.

The Lesson: Confidence doesn't come from removing every uncertainty. It comes from helping people feel capable of navigating it.

That's Regenerative Sales. We don't just teach reps how to move decisions forward. We teach them how to recognize the human conditions that make better decisions possible.

One of the biggest lessons I've learned from scaling a business is that growth exposes weaknesses faster than you expect.
  
When a business is relatively small, it's often possible to overcome challenges through hard work, flexibility and the determination of a few key individuals.
  
Processes don't always need to be perfect.
  
Systems can be relatively basic.
  
Decisions can be made quickly.
  
And people often take on responsibilities well beyond their job descriptions.
  
But as the business grows, that approach becomes increasingly difficult to sustain.
  
What worked for 5,000 customers doesn't necessarily work for 50,000.
  
And what worked for 50,000 may be completely unsuitable for 500,000.
  
Having been part of the journey of growing an energy business from a few thousand customers to more than a million, I've experienced those challenges firsthand.
  
The biggest mistake is assuming that more growth simply requires more of the same.
  
In reality, sustainable growth requires continual investment in:
  
• People and leadership capability
  
• Processes and operational efficiency
  
• Systems and technology
  
• Customer experience
  
• Management information and accountability
  
The businesses that scale successfully aren't necessarily those that avoid growing pains.
  
They're the ones that recognise the problems early and adapt before those problems become barriers to further growth.
  
Through SJ Parker Consulting, I help businesses assess their commercial and operational capability and identify what needs to change to support their next stage of growth.

A true leader understands that the success of their team is a reflection of their own leadership. They encourage people to grow, celebrate their achievements, acknowledge their contributions, and create an environment where everyone feels motivated to give their best.

Great leaders don’t compete with their team members; they empower them. They recognize that when individuals grow, the entire organization grows with them.

I have also learned an important lesson as a professional: focus on your work, not just on pleasing people.

Respect your seniors, value relationships, and remain open to feedback. At the same time, never lose your authenticity or compromise your values in the pursuit of approval.

Keep learning. Keep improving. Deliver your best with honesty, consistency, and integrity.

You may not always receive recognition when you expect it, and your journey may not always be easy. But don’t let external validation define your worth or determine your direction.

The most unreliable person in your startup is called “someone.”

The founders delivered dinner themselves.
In early 2013, a startup began testing delivery demand with a landing page and a phone number.
The founders had been speaking with local businesses in the Bay Area about what they needed to grow. Delivery challenges kept coming up.
So they started taking orders and doing most of the deliveries themselves.
By an investor interview on April 26, 2013, they had completed 217 deliveries.
Handling pickups and drop-offs helped them understand the practical difficulties of getting food to customers on time. They also spoke with customers, restaurants, and potential drivers.
The company went public in 2020.
Can you guess the company? 

Three lessons for founders:

1. Test the outcome before automating every step. Complete the service for a small group and record what breaks.
2. Talk to every participant. Customers, suppliers, and workers can experience different problems within the same transaction.
3. Track repeat use alongside delivery costs. Find out whether customers return and what it costs to serve them.

Before your next feature brief, pick one customer and complete the job with simple tools. Record the time, cost, and points of confusion.

Your AI may be saving time on paper while creating more work for your business.

The business may have accelerated one task without reducing the total workload.

Verification is necessary when mistakes carry serious consequences. But those requirements should be included when evaluating the technology's actual cost and value.

Before expanding an AI investment, leadership should ask:

Are we measuring real productivity improvements, or just how quickly the AI generates an answer?

INTYRE Decision Lab helps businesses examine operational and technology decisions when expected improvements aren't translating into actual results.

Your “we’ll automate that later” list is costing you $24,960 a year.

A client once showed me theirs. It was a yellow sticky note on their monitor. 
The corners had curled. It had been there for almost two years.

Three tasks. One of them was building the Monday sales report by hand.
Each one “only takes a few hours a week.”

So I did the maths with them:
12 hours a week.
× $40 an hour.
× 52 weeks.
$24,960.

They went quiet. Then they said: “That’s almost a part-time hire.”

It’s not just the money. It’s the Friday evenings spent catching up, and the work that only gets done because one person stays late.

Here’s how I clear that list:

→ Write every task down. The annoying 10-minute ones add up fastest.

→ Put a yearly cost next to each. Hours × rate × 52. It makes the list impossible to ignore.

→ Ignore ROI for the first one. Most consultants will tell you to start with the most expensive task. I don’t. I start with the one the team hates most. The first automation isn’t about money. It’s about getting your team to trust it.

→ Automate that one this month. One task, done properly. Then the next.
By week six, all three tasks were automated. Their team got back 9 of those 12 hours every week, and they brought me the next three tasks themselves.

“Later” was the most expensive word in their business.

What’s on your sticky note?

AI can improve efficiency. But expecting immediate productivity leaps often leads to disappointment. 

Many organizations launch AI initiatives with ambitious targets. In practice, most projects fail to create measurable value because the underlying foundation is missing. Sustainable efficiency gains require reliable data, stable processes, and clear responsibilities. 

"The real challenge is not introducing AI but identifying where it creates the highest operational impact," states Leila Ali Cavasonza, Manager at Porsche Consulting. Some applications address infrequent but critical issues with major business consequences. Others automate small repetitive tasks performed thousands of times each day. Both approaches can generate significant value when applied in the right context. Several examples already demonstrate this potential: 

➡️ In airport operations, AI supported causal analysis helps identify the root causes of delays across highly interconnected systems involving airlines, ground handling, and service providers. 

➡️ In logistics, forecasting models improve demand planning, inventory management, and operational resilience through scenario simulation. 

➡️ In administrative functions, repetitive activities such as invoice matching and document processing can be automated to reduce manual effort and improve process speed. 

The impact varies by use case. Strategic improvements can fundamentally change operational performance. Smaller efficiency gains at process level become highly relevant when scaled across entire organizations. Successful implementation depends on more than technology alone. Clear ownership, strong collaboration across functions, and high quality data remain essential for scalable results.

Your healthcare AI startup could save clinicians hundreds of hours and still lose the contract because you haven't saved the hospital a single dollar. This came up again today, so I'm posting this.

This is one of the most expensive commercial mistakes I see healthcare AI founders make.

They calculate hours saved, multiply them by clinician salaries and call it ROI.

For example, if your AI saves 1,000 clinician hours at an average loaded cost of $150 per hour, you claim $150,000 in savings.

1,000 hours × $150 = $150,000.

The founder sees $150,000 in savings.

The CFO sees $150,000 in theoretical productivity and absolutely nothing coming off the payroll.

Your pitch deck says $150,000 saved.

The hospital's P&L says $0.

And the CFO has one question.

"Which line on my P&L actually changes?"

If you can't answer that, your ROI calculation is worthless as evidence of financial savings.
Unless those hours reduce overtime, avoid additional hires or generate profitable patient encounters, you haven't demonstrated a financial return.

You've demonstrated time saved.

And that's the difference between a product clinicians love and a contract the CFO will actually approve.

Your clinical champion loves the product. The pilot works. But without a credible financial return, your successful pilot risks becoming another stalled contract.

So here's what I'd recommend.

Before starting a pilot, agree with the CFO on a measurable financial outcome.

Establish the baseline and track actual reductions in overtime or agency spending, avoided hiring costs, or additional contribution margin from increased patient volume.

Subtract software, implementation, training and ongoing operating costs.

Now you've got a credible basis for calculating financial ROI.

Clinical productivity matters. Better working conditions matter. Giving clinicians more time with patients matters.

But those benefits aren't automatically financial savings.

And if your entire commercial proposition depends on savings that never materialize, you don't have a product performance problem.

You have a business model that may not survive procurement.

No amount of AI innovation will fix a commercial proposition built on financial returns the customer cannot realize.

The AI ROI Paradox: We’re getting better at measuring what AI does. Are we getting better at measuring what it changes?

The most expensive part of an AI interaction may happen after it ends.
A 2025 field study published in the Quarterly Journal of Economics found that AI assistance increased support agents’ productivity by 15%, measured in issues resolved per hour. 
McKinsey’s 2026 State of AI found that 80% of respondents reported higher individual productivity, while 37% attributed any positive EBIT impact to AI.

Different measures, certainly but they expose a question worth asking.

In Customer Experience, a conversation can end while the customer’s problem continues. What looks like successful deflection may return as another contact, a complex escalation, or recovery work for Customer Success.

That work can disappear from one dashboard and reappear in another.
The reverse matters, too. Freed-up capacity might allow a team to absorb growth, handle complex cases better, or reduce customer effort- even without an immediate payroll reduction. That can create real value, but it isn't the same as cash saved.
A credible AI business case should follow the work beyond the interaction: What stayed resolved? What came back? What did we actually save or improve?

If the ROI calculation ends when the AI interaction ends, we might be measuring a handoff rather than a saving.

AI Adoption Is Not the Same as Business Transformation

Almost every business conversation today seems to include Artificial Intelligence.

Companies are exploring AI, investing in tools, running pilot projects and talking about automation.

But I have a question:

Are companies adopting AI because it is genuinely improving their business, or simply because they don't want to be left behind?

There is a difference between adopting technology and creating business value through technology.

In my view, this is a question that deserves attention not just from management, but also from the boardroom.

A few questions worth asking:

- What specific business problem are we trying to solve through AI?
- Will it reduce costs, improve productivity or create new revenue opportunities?
- How will we measure whether the investment is successful?
- Are our employees prepared to work with these new tools?
- What about customer data, privacy, security and accountability?
- If the technology makes a wrong decision, who is responsible?

The board does not need to decide which AI tool the company should purchase.

That is an operational decision.

But the board should ensure that the investment has a clear purpose, measurable outcomes and appropriate safeguards.

Technology investments should not be driven by excitement alone.

They should be driven by business needs.

I believe the companies that benefit most from AI will not necessarily be those that adopt it first, but those that understand where to use it, how to measure its value and how to manage its risks.

The real question is not whether our company is using AI. It is whether AI is making our company better.

Not Every AI Use Case Deserves a Budget. Here's How to Decide.
AI is exciting. But excitement doesn't equal business value. One of the biggest mistakes organizations make is investing in AI solutions before determining whether they're solving the right problem. Just because AI can do something doesn't mean your business should invest in it. Before approving your next AI initiative, ask a few questions: 

🎯 1. Business Value: What measurable problem are we solving? Will this reduce costs, increase revenue, or improve customer experience?
⚙️ 2. Implementation Effort: How difficult will this be to implement and integrate into existing workflows?
📊 3. Data Readiness: Do we have the quality, accessible data needed to make this successful?
🛡️ 4. Risk & Governance: What are the security, compliance, and operational risks?
⏱️ 5. Time to Value: How quickly can we demonstrate meaningful results?

Here's a practical example: A customer service team is considering two AI initiatives:
Option A: An AI chatbot that handles routine customer inquiries.
Option B: An AI-powered analytics solution that predicts customer churn.

Both have potential. But which one should receive funding first? The answer depends on business priorities, implementation readiness, expected ROI, and risk—not which technology sounds more impressive.

💡 My takeaway: The best AI strategy doesn't start with selecting tools. It starts with identifying and prioritizing the right business opportunities.

Clara Raises $105 Million: The Race to Reinvent Corporate Finance in Latin America

The future of fintech may not be built around consumer payments alone. Increasingly, investors are backing platforms that help businesses manage the complexity of money itself.

Clara, a five-year-old São Paulo-based fintech startup, has secured $105 million in fresh financing to expand its corporate financial management business.

The funding comprises a $65 million Series C round anchored by Citius, Kaszek Ventures, and DEG, alongside $40 million in renewed growth financing from General Catalyst's Customer Value Fund.

Clara helps businesses manage corporate spending, invoices, bills, and cross-border payments through an integrated financial platform.

The problem it is addressing is significant. Businesses operating across Latin America often navigate fragmented payment systems, complex financial administration, and cross-border transaction challenges.

Clara's proposition is to bring these financial operations together, giving companies greater visibility and control over their spending.

But the bigger story is the growing confidence of investors in Latin America's fintech infrastructure.

While much of the global AI and technology conversation focuses on consumer-facing applications, companies like Clara are targeting the operational foundations of business: payments, financial visibility, expense management, and cash-flow efficiency.

For emerging markets, this development carries an important lesson.

The next generation of valuable fintech companies may not simply be those helping people move money. They may be the companies rebuilding how businesses manage, monitor, and deploy capital.

The future of fintech belongs to platforms that solve real financial infrastructure problems, not just those that make transactions faster.

Rigged Wednesday | Why VCs pass on good businesses

Your business can be good and still be unfundable. Here's why.

Venture math runs on the power law: a few investments have to return the whole fund. So every VC asks one question above all: can this be one of those?

A profitable company growing 30% a year is a great business. It's also a bad venture bet, because it can't carry a fund by itself.

When a VC says no, often they mean "not venture-shaped." Not "bad company."

The right capital for a good-but-not-viral business is out there: angels, revenue-based financing, customer prepayments, plain profit.

Picking the wrong capital for your shape is how good companies get broken.

Introducing: The Economics of Entrepreneurship
Entrepreneurship is often discussed in terms of innovation, funding, disruption, and success stories.
But there is a deeper dimension that deserves more attention: the economics and psychology behind entrepreneurial decisions.
Why do some startups succeed despite limited resources, while others fail despite significant funding?
Why do investors sometimes follow market sentiment rather than economic fundamentals?
How do behavioral biases influence founders' decisions, risk-taking, and strategic choices?
And perhaps most importantly, how can economic thinking help entrepreneurs build sustainable and scalable businesses?
These questions inspired me to launch a new series:
"The Economics of Entrepreneurship"
Through this series, I will explore the intersection of:
Economic Thinking: Markets, incentives, productivity, resource allocation, and value creation.
Behavioral Economics: Decision-making, cognitive biases, risk perception, and human behavior.
Venture Capital & Investment: Capital allocation, startup valuation, investment strategies, and financial sustainability.
Entrepreneurial Strategy: Business models, scalability, competitive advantage, and long-term growth.
My objective is to go beyond conventional entrepreneurship discussions and examine the economic forces and behavioral patterns shaping the entrepreneurial ecosystem.
Because entrepreneurship is not just about building companies.
It is about understanding how people make decisions, how markets create opportunities, and how resources can be transformed into sustainable economic value.
I look forward to sharing insights, challenging assumptions, and opening meaningful discussions.
Let's rethink entrepreneurship through the lens of economics.

Building a #B2B #marketing #strategy before running any campaigns is like hiring a sales team before you know whether anyone wants to buy. 🎯

You’re guessing what the market needs, what messaging will land, and which offer will convert.

The better way: build the strategy on live-tested assumptions.
That means launching small campaigns before the strategy is finalised.

Every assumption can now be tested in a live environment, on Google Ads, Meta, LinkedIn, or even ChatGPT.

Here’s the simplified process:
- What worked before? Keep it in. But remember: it can change. 📉
- List as many assumptions as possible. Then evaluate each one.
- Test the top 10 assumptions with a 2-week campaign, as if that campaign were the strategy.

Don’t measure “real results” yet. Measure whether there’s demand, whether that demand is catchable, and whether people who land on your site actually engage.

In other words: did this assumption show any traction that could lead to sales?

Only then write the strategy. And if new assumptions emerge, repeat the testing.

NB! Not all marketing strategies are online activities. But all ideas can be tested online. 💯🌶️

A strategy that has never met the market is just a beautifully formatted opinion.

Test first. Strategise second.

Angel Investors vs Venture Capitalists: What's the Difference?

Behind many growing startups are investors who believe in their potential and provide the financial support needed to turn ideas into businesses.

Two important participants in the startup funding ecosystem are Angel Investors and Venture Capitalists (VCs).

Angel Investors are individuals who invest their personal money in early-stage startups. Apart from funding, they may also offer mentorship, industry connections and business guidance.

Venture Capitalists, on the other hand, are professional investors or investment firms that invest pooled funds in startups with significant growth potential, usually in exchange for equity.

Here are some key differences:

1. Source of Funds: Angel investors use personal wealth, while VCs invest funds managed on behalf of investors.
2. Investment Stage: Angels often support early-stage ventures, while VCs may invest in startups at different growth stages.
3. Investment Size: Angel investments are generally smaller than venture capital investments.
4. Decision-Making: Angel investors may make individual investment decisions, while VC firms usually follow a structured evaluation process.

Both play an important role in helping startups access capital, expertise and opportunities.

Remember: Angel investors may help a startup take its first steps, while venture capital can help it pursue larger ambitions.

I once watched a sales team pivot from chasing every new lead to nurturing a handful of high‑intent prospects. They mapped the trade‑off between volume and conversion, then tightened their funnel.

First, they identified the “sweet spot” where lead quality met resource capacity. That meant dropping 30 % of low‑intent contacts and reallocating effort to the top 10 %.

Second, they built a simple scorecard: engagement depth, buying signals, and fit. Every touchpoint was logged, and the scorecard fed into a real‑time dashboard.

Third, they instituted a weekly review loop. The team examined which touchpoints lifted scores and which stalled progress, then tweaked messaging or timing.

Result? The conversion rate rose, and the sales cycle shortened by roughly a week. The key was a disciplined trade‑off map that turned chaotic outreach into a focused, repeatable habit.

What trade‑off map is your team using to turn demand into durable revenue?

Some of the most important leadership lessons I've learned happened when things weren't going according to plan.
Not during training.
Not in a meeting.
But on those days when customers were waiting, systems weren't cooperating, deadlines were approaching, and everyone needed answers.
Working in banking operations for over a decade taught me that leadership is often tested when you have very little time to make a decision.
And in those moments, I've learned that three things matter.
1. Clarity before urgency.
Not every urgent situation requires an immediate reaction.
Sometimes, taking a moment to understand the actual problem prevents hours of unnecessary corrections.
2. Accountability without blame.
When something goes wrong, the priority should be understanding what happened, resolving the issue, and preventing it from recurring.
There will always be time to review individual responsibilities, but blame rarely fixes an operational problem.
3. Communication that creates confidence.
People don't always expect you to have every answer immediately.
But they need to know that someone understands the situation, is taking responsibility, and is working toward a resolution.
These lessons have stayed with me as I've moved into data analytics, business operations, and leadership within a growing startup.
Because whether you're managing a banking operation, coordinating a project, or leading an analytics team, the fundamentals remain surprisingly similar.
Understand the problem. Make an informed decision. Communicate clearly. Take responsibility. Learn from the outcome.
I've come to appreciate that leadership isn't measured only by how well things run when everything is working.
It's also reflected in how we respond when things aren't.
Pressure doesn't automatically make someone a better leader. But it can reveal the habits they've built.

What can leaders take away from the recent headlines?

Jensen Huang, CEO and Founder of NVIDIA, has resigned after 33 years. The facts and circumstances are troubling on many fronts, but that's for the nightly news.

A review of this situation raises four things every leadership team should be discussing:

1️⃣ Succession planning is important! If your answer to “who is next” is “we will figure it out,” you have a problem on your hands.  Prudent management necessitates this "boring" topic be a part of regular board and management discussions;

2️⃣ Governance strategies and structures should get built before you need them. Who can remove the CEO. Who investigates. Who chairs the room. Build the plan while everything is going well;

3️⃣ When the leader is the brand, the leader is the - or one of the - existential risks. Founders are often the best salesperson in the company.  The goal isn’t to make your best seller less visible. It’s to make sure the customers know and trust the team behind them too; and

A single card changed the entire energy of a training room. 🃏
Recently, I led a series of GIP product training sessions with our sales teams in Delhi. 📍
Anyone who has attended corporate training knows the default setting: one-way slides, polite nods, and half the room quietly glancing at their phones. 📱
So I decided to try something different. Instead of running a one-way presentation, I turned the session into a game. 🎯
Here’s how the Card Technique worked:
🃏 Every time someone participated or answered a question, I handed them a card.
✅ It didn’t matter whether their answer was right or wrong—participation itself earned the card.
🏆 At the end of the session, whoever collected the most cards won.
The shift in the room was immediate. ⚡
Hesitation turned into raised hands. Passive listeners became active participants. 🙌
There’s simple psychology behind why this works: gamification and immediate positive reinforcement. 🧠 Introduce small rewards, clear points, and a touch of friendly competition, and people stop waiting for a session to end—they start owning the learning process.
There’s a bigger lesson here for marketers and business leaders, too: 💡
Engagement rarely comes from giving people more information.
It comes from changing how they experience that information.
Don’t just deliver a presentation. Design an experience. ✨
Big thanks to our Delhi teams for bringing such great energy to the sessions! 👏

When I first started learning sales, I thought being good at conversations meant knowing what to ask next. But the more I practise, the more I realise that it’s not about having a long list of questions. It’s about understanding the person sitting across from you.

If a prospect tells me they’re struggling to get clients, I shouldn’t immediately jump to the next question on my list. I should be curious enough to explore why, how long it’s been happening and what they’ve tried so far.

Presence, conversational awareness and active listening are skills to prioritize. I’m learning to stop treating discovery like an interview and start treating it like a genuine conversation.

It’s not about asking more questions. It’s about asking questions that help me understand more. That’s a skill I’m working on every day.

#SalesJourney #HighTicketSales #DiscoveryCalls #ConsultativeSelling #PersonalGrowth

There are many different sales methodologies, personalities and philosophies. Some emphasize negotiation, others storytelling, value creation, active listening or understanding customer psychology. But I believe the most successful salespeople share a number of fundamental principles.

1️⃣ Understand the customer before presenting your solution. Know their business, market, challenges, priorities and strategic objectives. The better you understand their reality, the more relevant your value proposition becomes.

2️⃣ Sell outcomes, not specifications. Customers are rarely interested in technical features for their own sake. They want to understand what those features mean for their business. Translate product capabilities into measurable value, reduced risk and better outcomes.

3️⃣ Listen more than you speak. The best sales conversations are not presentations. They are dialogues. Listen carefully and pay attention to what customers are not explicitly saying.

4️⃣ Build trust before asking for commitment. Trust is earned through expertise, consistency, transparency and reliability. Especially in complex B2B environments, relationships are built over time, not through a single successful sales meeting.

5️⃣ Turn objections into opportunities. An objection is often an indication of an unanswered question, an unmet need or a perceived risk. Instead of defending yourself, understand what is behind the objection.

6️⃣ Demonstrate value before discussing price. When customers clearly understand the value you create, the conversation changes. Price becomes one part of the decision rather than the entire decision.

7️⃣ Make the buying decision easier. Reduce uncertainty and help customers navigate complexity. Your role is not to push a decision but to give customers the confidence and information they need to make one.

8️⃣ Know your product, but understand your customer’s business even better. Product expertise gives you credibility. Business understanding makes you relevant. The combination creates a much stronger foundation for strategic partnerships.

9️⃣ Think beyond the next transaction. Winning an order is a sales achievement. Becoming a trusted partner who contributes to your customer’s long-term success is a business development achievement.


I believe the biggest difference between transactional selling and strategic business development is the starting point.

Transactional selling starts with:
💡 What can I sell to this customer?

Strategic selling starts with:
💡What can I help this customer achieve?

That shift changes the entire relationship. It influences how we approach customers, how we create value, how we develop our offering and ultimately how we build sustainable business. The best salespeople don’t just sell products. They build confidence, create value and earn the right to be part of their customers’ future.

What 25 Years in B2B Sales Has Taught Me About Closing Deals
After 25 years in sales, I've learned that closing deals isn't about having the perfect pitch, memorizing clever responses, or pushing harder.
It's about mastering the fundamentals of professional selling.

Here are five lessons that have shaped my approach:
1. You Don't Have to Win Every Deal.
Not every prospect is the right fit. Know when to walk away and focus your time on opportunities worth pursuing.
2. Never Discount Before Understanding the Objection.
When a prospect says your price is too high, find out why. Is it the budget, perceived value, or comparison to another solution? Understand before you negotiate.
3. Prevent Objections Before They Happen.
Don't wait until closing to discover what's holding your prospect back. Uncover concerns about price, timing, value, and decision-making early.
4. Focus on What You Can Control.
You can't control whether someone buys. You can control your prospecting, preparation, appointments, and follow-up. Consistency in these activities creates opportunities.
5. Build Trust Instead of Applying Pressure.
People want to feel confident about the person they're doing business with. Build trust through preparation, honesty, listening, and consistency.

The Bigger Lesson
Closing isn't a single moment at the end of a sales conversation. It's the result of everything you've done before that moment.
How you prepare, qualify, communicate value, and build trust all contribute to earning the business.
The best salespeople don't just know how to ask for the business. They know how to earn it.
Sales is a profession. Treat it like one.

Your sales script is brilliant.

Until the prospect starts behaving like a human being. 😂

During a coaching session, I gave a salesperson an unfamiliar £5,000 offer.

No script. Just a framework.
I played the prospect.
Vague answers. Contradictions. Unexpected questions.

Absolute chaos. Apparently.

But something interesting happened.

She stopped trying to remember what to say and started actually listening.

Was it perfect? Not even close.

Did she uncover the prospect's problems, motivations and desired outcome?

Absolutely.

And that's the lesson.

Scripts teach salespeople what to say.
Coaching teaches them how to think.

If your rep falls apart the moment a prospect goes off-script, you've trained a performer, not a salesperson.

Stop building human teleprompters. Start developing salespeople.

That's Aletheia. 🔱

Wanna know why your sales associates can be polite and still not convert any sales?

Because ATTENDING to a customer and SELLING to a customer are two different approaches. Most retail stores only train for the first.

Here are 4 methods you can teach your team today:

1. THE INQUIRY
ATTENDING ~ Welcomes the client and simply answers the questions asked.
SELLING ~ Welcomes the client, then asks: "What's the occasion?"
Difference: Client relationships start with knowing what they like. That's what keeps them happy and coming back.

2. THE PRESENTATION
ATTENDING ~ Shows what's on the rack.
SELLING ~ Pieces together options that match what the client needs.
Difference: You simplify their shopping by giving them a few options to choose from.

3. THE GUIDE
ATTENDING ~ Waits for the customer to decide.
SELLING ~ Helps the customer decide with confidence, without pushing. E.g.: "Which of these do you see yourself being more comfortable in?"
Difference: The decision feels like theirs, not yours.

4. THE FOLLOW-UP
ATTENDING ~ Ends at the till.
SELLING ~ Continues the relationship after the till with a follow-up.
Difference: The customer knows they spent money. A simple call or text reminds them of the value they got.

A friendly team that only attends will keep customers comfortable. A team that sells will keep them coming back.

Which one is your team doing today?

One of the harder parts of leadership must be knowing when not to lead from the front. 

This piece from MIT Sloan Executive Education introduces an idea I really like: “Step Up, Step Back.” Leaders get closely involved at the beginning of change, setting the direction, priorities, and strategy, but then intentionally step back to give teams ownership of making it happen.  

It made me think about how easily involvement can become over-involvement. 

Being visible and engaged matters. But so does trusting people to solve problems, make decisions, and find the best route forward themselves. 

Maybe great leadership during change isn’t about being present at every turn. It’s about creating enough clarity at the start that you don’t need to be.

Sales lessons from 24 years in the game
  
If I could go back and give my 18 year old self a few pointers, I'd probably start with these.
  
▶️ Stop trying to sell to everyone. Not every prospect is the right prospect. Spend your time where you can genuinely add value.
▶️ Listen more than you talk. The best salespeople aren't necessarily the best talkers. They're the ones who ask the right questions and actually listen to the answers.
▶️ Your reputation walks into the room before you do. People remember how you treat them, particularly when things don't go to plan.
▶️ Follow up. You'd be amazed how many opportunities are lost simply because someone didn't pick up the phone or send that second email.
▶️ Don't confuse being busy with being productive. A full diary doesn't necessarily mean a full pipeline.
▶️ Learn to take rejection. Not every conversation becomes a deal. Don't take it personally. Learn, move on and keep going.
▶️ Look after your relationships. Today's prospect could be tomorrow's biggest      opportunity. And sometimes the person who can't help you today becomes the person who opens the biggest door tomorrow.
  
And perhaps the biggest lesson of all…
You don't have to be the cleverest person in the room. You just need to be someone people trust, respect and want to do business with.
  
I've made plenty of mistakes along the way. Probably still making a few!
But 24 years on, I genuinely believe the fundamentals of good sales haven't changed that much.
  
Technology changes. Products change. Markets change.
 🔝 Relationships still matter.
  
What advice would you give your 18 year old self?

💡 Some of the most effective sales frameworks are also the simplest.
One of them is Problem → Impact → Solution.

Instead of jumping straight into your product, guide the prospect through three steps:

1️⃣ Problem — What challenge are they actually facing?
2️⃣ Impact — How is that problem affecting their business, time, costs, or results?
3️⃣ Solution — What needs to change, and how can you help them get there?

The key is the second step.

A problem alone doesn't always create urgency. When prospects understand what that problem is costing them, solving it becomes much more important.

Great sales conversations don't overwhelm people with features and presentations, they create clarity around the problem, make the impact visible, and show a clear path forward.

Don't start by explaining what you sell. Start by understanding what needs to be solved.

People don't buy presentations, they buy solutions to problems that matter.

#Sales #SalesStrategy #ProblemSolving #B2BSales #ConsultativeSelling #SalesMindsHub

Most sales calls are won or lost before the price ever comes up.

By that point, the prospect has already decided whether they feel understood.

Every habit I’ve built around sales calls comes back to that one thing.

I always go for video. Seeing how someone reacts tells me when to slow down, when to dig deeper and when they’re ready to move forward.

My camera stays on. People buy from people they can see and trust.

I start with discovery, every time. Until I know where someone is coming from, I have nothing worth pitching.

I follow a simple structure. It keeps the conversation heading in the right direction and still leaves room for it to feel natural.

And I send the proposal afterwards. Giving someone space to think it through builds real trust, and trust is what turns a good call into a client.

Simple habits, all built around the person on the other side of the call.

Your team's next breakthrough might not require another tool.

It might require a different way of thinking.

Sales and marketing teams have more data, technology, and resources at their fingertips than ever before.

But even with all that information, some of the most important questions remain unanswered.

• Why aren't customers responding the way we expected?
 • What assumptions are shaping our strategies?
 • Are we solving the problems that actually matter to the people we're trying to reach?

That's where consumer psychology can change the conversation.

#ConsumerPsychology 
#BuyerBehavior 
#MarketingStrategy 
#UnfairAdvantage 
#TheBuycologist

A customer can want your product and still choose not to buy it.

And sometimes, the problem isn't your price.

It's your message.

Think about it.

A customer sees your product. They're interested. They ask questions and consider buying.

But your message keeps talking about how good your product is without addressing what the customer is worried about.

They want to know:

Will this product solve my problem?

Is it worth my money?

Can I trust this business?

What if it doesn't meet my expectations?


When these concerns remain unanswered, hesitation grows.

This is why understanding customer psychology matters in marketing.

People don't just want to hear what you're selling. They want to understand how it meets their needs and why they should feel confident buying it.

Good marketing doesn't just promote a product. It addresses the questions holding customers back from buying.

Before writing your next marketing message, ask yourself:

Am I communicating what my business wants to sell, or what my customer needs to hear?

That's a difference worth paying attention to.

Customers can tell when you're listening for yourself

You ask a question

They start explaining

And while they're talking, you're already thinking:

"That's useful"
"I can sell them X"
"That gives me an angle"
"Wait until I tell them about..."

Technically, you're listening

But who are you listening for?

Chapter 4 of Selling Through Partnering Skills explored trust as one of the six elements of PQ (Partnering Intelligence) 

I used something that has remained part of my work ever since:

The Trust Equation (developed by David Maister, Charles Green and Robert Galford)

Trust is influenced by:

Credibility + Reliability + Intimacy
divided by:
Self-orientation

In simple terms:

Do you know your stuff? 
Do you do what you say you'll do?
Do I feel safe dealing with you?
And...
How much is this really about you?

That last one matters

Because salespeople can do all the apparently right things while still being highly self-oriented

We can ask questions because we want information that helps us sell
We can listen because we're waiting for the gap where we can introduce our solution
We can build relationships because we've calculated that relationships improve conversion
We can even talk enthusiastically about being customer-centric because being customer-centric is good for target

Customers aren't stupid

They notice

In the book I asked whether we're listening simply to gather data for our own purposes... or whether we're listening to genuinely hear the customer

Six years later, I think that's an even bigger question

Because the tools available to salespeople have become considerably more sophisticated so we can 

Research customers better
Generate insights
Prepare better questions
Analyse conversations
Produce impressive proposals

AI can help us do all of that

Great stuff...  but none of it changes a fairly basic human judgement:

Do I believe this person is genuinely interested in helping me make a good decision?

Perhaps that's why trust isn't really something you build with a clever technique

It's something your behaviour gives people reason to place in you

So here's a useful question before your next customer conversation:

Who am I listening for?

Bruno Miguel Pinto Figueiredo This resonates. One of the most important leadership lessons I’ve learned is to develop people who can lead without me. Decentralization of command and authority is paramount.

That requires the courage to step back, the discipline to establish clear standards, and the trust to give people genuine ownership. Ask questions that strengthen judgment, welcome challenge, and give people room to make decisions—with support and accountability.

The real test comes when you’re absent. Can your people think critically, act decisively, and move the mission forward? Building that capability is a leader’s responsibility.

Strong performance doesn't always lead to greater leadership opportunities. Being good at your job and being recognized as someone who can lead at the next level are two different things.

Uma Subramanian, author of The Sought-After Leader: Why Great Isn't Enough and How to Rise Above It, draws on more than 20 years in the tech industry, including two decades at Microsoft, to explore what it takes to move beyond individual performance.

We discuss why visibility doesn't have to mean self-promotion, how leaders can build genuine influence without playing office politics, and why the transition from individual contributor to people leader requires a different set of skills. POV: YOU OPENED A SHOPPING APP JUST TO BROWSE. 😭


10 minutes later:
7 products in your cart.
3 things you didn't know existed five minutes ago.
1 discount you absolutely cannot miss.

₹2,000 worth of things you never planned to buy. 💀

And your original mission?
Buying a ₹200 notebook. 🤡

WELCOME TO THE WORLD OF IMPULSE BUYING. 🛍️

But why does this happen?

Let's understand the psychology behind it. 🧠👇🏻

1. THE EXCITEMENT OF SOMETHING NEW

Finding something attractive can create an immediate desire to own it. 

Sometimes, the excitement of buying feels more appealing than thinking about whether we actually need the product.

2. SEEING IT CHANGES EVERYTHING

You weren't looking for that cute phone case until it appeared on your screen.

Sometimes, exposure to a product creates a desire that wasn't there before. 

Attractive displays, appealing product images, and personalised recommendations can all influence what catches our attention.

3. THE FEAR OF MISSING OUT

"ONLY 2 LEFT!"
"SALE ENDS TONIGHT!"

Suddenly, waiting feels risky. 

What if the product sells out? 
What if the offer disappears?

The possibility of missing out can make us act faster than we otherwise would.

BUT HERE'S THE INTERESTING PART. 🧠

Impulse buying isn't simply about having poor self-control.

Our emotions, surroundings, and the way products are presented can all influence our purchasing decisions.

For marketers, understanding these behaviours helps explain why product placement, recommendations, and promotional messages can influence what customers consider buying.

Of course, influence isn't the same as control. 

Not every customer responds to the same technique, and not every unplanned purchase is a bad decision.

The real value lies in understanding WHY we buy, not just WHAT we buy.

So, the next time you add something unexpected to your cart, ask yourself:

"Did I want this before I saw it, or did I start wanting it after I saw it?" 👀

💬 LET'S TALK!

What's the most random thing you've ever bought on impulse? 
And be honest—did you regret it later, or was it actually worth it? 😂👇🏻

So You Want to Start Your Own Business? Let’s Talk About It. 🚀

Last week I had the opportunity to host a breakout session for ICSC ’s Next Generation Leadership Network on starting your own business.

Since launching PULSE Real Estate Strategies last year, I’ve learned that entrepreneurship is equal parts strategy, resilience, adaptability, and a little delusion.

There’s no perfect roadmap, but there are plenty of lessons worth sharing. Here’s the condensed version of my very unofficial 13-step startup guide:

CHAPTER 1 | THE LEAP

1. Listen to the Ping. That idea that keeps resurfacing? Pay attention to it.
2. Don’t Overthink It. Do your homework, make informed decisions, and take action. Perfectionism can quickly become analysis paralysis.
3. Be a Little Delusional. Confidence doesn’t replace strategy, but you do have to believe before there’s proof.

CHAPTER 2 | THE FOUNDATION

4. Build a Business Plan. (This one is obvious.)
5. Do Your Research. Market demand, competitors, clients, business names, domains, trademarks. Think beyond launch.
6. Establish Your Business Entity. Understand your legal and tax options. Consult professionals.
7. Build Your Budget. Then Triple It. Plan for unexpected expenses, delayed payments, and slower growth. Revenue ≠ cash flow.

CHAPTER 3 | BUILD & LAUNCH

8. Build Your Infrastructure. Website, contracts, accounting, CRM, marketing. Know when to outsource, but don’t overspend before validating demand.
9. Just Launch.  Your first version won’t be your final version. Get into the market and start learning.
10. Ask for Help & Feedback. Learn from founders, mentors, clients, and advisors. You don’t have to figure everything out alone, but be mindful of whose advice you take.
11. Tweak, Refine & Evolve. Adapt as you learn.

CHAPTER 4 | THE REALITY

12. Prepare for the “Oh F***” Phase.The excitement is real. So are the unexpected challenges. Resilience is part of the business plan. Consider it a rite of passage.
13. Cut Out the Noise. Everyone will have opinions. Stay open to learning, but don’t let someone else’s fears, limitations, or priorities dictate your vision. A lot of people operate from a place of fear and scarcity. Learn to recognize it without absorbing it. Protect your energy. Remember why you started.

THE BIGGEST TAKEAWAY?

Starting a business isn’t just about building a company. It’s about building something aligned with your strengths, values, ambitions, and the life you actually want to live.

It will grow and stretch you in so many ways. Some beautiful, some difficult, and often both at once.

It’s not for everyone. 
But it’s definitely for me 🥰

There’s a lot brewing behind the scenes at PULSE! I’m having so much fun building and creating, and I can’t wait to share what’s coming and the value I hope to bring to our industry and communities. 

For my fellow entrepreneurs, what are your thoughts? What else would you add to the list?

What if your company supported you in leaving your job to build your own startup, and welcomed you back if it failed? 🚀

That’s the idea behind iD Fresh Food’s entrepreneurship policy, introduced by its Global CEO, Musthafa P.C.

Instead of treating employee departures as a loss, the company is creating a pathway for employees to become entrepreneurs.

Here’s what makes this initiative different:

💰 1. Financial support
Employees can receive a partially paid sabbatical while working on their business ideas.

🤝 2. Mentorship from leadership
They can learn from experienced leaders who understand the challenges of building a business.

🌐 3. Access to a business network
Employees can tap into the company’s ecosystem and partner network to help develop their ventures.

🔄 4. A second chance if things go wrong
If their entrepreneurial journey doesn’t work out, they have the option to approach the company about returning.

The policy reflects Musthafa’s own journey. iD Fresh Food began in a small Bengaluru kitchen with an initial investment of just ₹50,000.

Now, the company wants to extend that spirit of entrepreneurship to its employees.

The bigger lesson for businesses?

You don’t have to lose talented people simply because they dream of building something of their own.

Sometimes, supporting their ambitions can create more value than asking them to stay on a conventional career path.

Imagine how many great businesses could exist if more employees had the confidence to take that first step.

Would you leave a stable job to build your own startup if you had this kind of safety net?

Entrepreneurship means responsibility. But who takes care of the entrepreneur?

Sometimes, in quiet moments, I ask myself: What am I actually doing?

A year ago, I was still employed, earning a regular salary. Today, I’m building several business areas without investors and with a limited budget.

I work with people from different professional backgrounds. I’m constantly learning new things, from technology and website hosting to GitHub and artificial intelligence. I question my strategies, review every expense and keep adapting.

You have to generate new business, make sure people get paid, motivate your team and lead by example.

You carry responsibility for people who rely on you.

And you can’t simply share all your worries and doubts with your employees. They also need guidance, motivation and someone who leads with confidence.

My biggest lesson in recent weeks?

You need your weekends for yourself!

Get outside. Spend time in nature. Recharge your batteries. Surround yourself with positive people. Meet people you can talk to about something other than business, revenue and the next strategy.

Because entrepreneurial responsibility doesn’t simply disappear on Friday evening. But you have to learn to give yourself permission to switch off.

Otherwise, you might build a successful business while losing yourself in the process.

That’s one lesson I’d like to share with other entrepreneurs and startup founders.

Revenue growth does not guarantee valuation growth. And AI is changing the economics behind both.
  
“Are we building a business that buyers will pay MORE for—or funding growth that deserves a LOWER valuation multiple?”
  
Here are 10 questions every PE operating partner, investor and portfolio-company board should be asking NOW:
  
1. REVENUE QUALITY: Are we increasing valuable, profitable ARR—or simply adding revenue at any cost?
  
2. AI DISRUPTION: Will AI strengthen our competitive moat, or make our product easier to replicate and cheaper to replace?
  
3. CUSTOMER RETENTION: Are we acquiring new customers to disguise declining NRR, weak expansion or growing churn?
  
4. GTM EFFICIENCY: Are additional sales and marketing investments generating profitable growth—or scaling inefficiency?
  
5. REVENUE PREDICTABILITY: Can management substantiate its next four quarters of revenue, or are forecasts based on optimistic pipeline assumptions?
  
6. PRICING POWER: If AI reduces customer headcount and software seats, how will we preserve or increase revenue per customer?
  
7. CUSTOMER PROFITABILITY: Are our largest customers also our most profitable—or are hidden delivery, support and AI costs destroying margins?
  
8. MARKET RELEVANCE: Would we underwrite the same TAM, competitive position and growth assumptions if we made this investment today?
  
9. SCALABILITY: Can this business grow predictably without continually increasing headcount, spending or founder involvement?
  
10. EXIT READINESS: What three weaknesses would a prospective acquirer use TODAY to justify a lower purchase multiple?
  
MY CHALLENGE TO PE FIRMS AND PORTFOLIO BOARDS:
  
If your SaaS company executes its current operating plan perfectly for the next 24 months, will its enterprise value increase enough to meet your investment thesis?

The 30% rule for predictable sales

Last week, I read *DM to Deals* by Allan Miles. Its chapter on predictable sales resonated with me because I’ve used this approach for more than 20 years.

Many professional salespeople understand the numbers behind their sales process. But business owners may not know their conversion rates—or may not use them to plan.

Knowing the relationship between each stage of your sales process helps you work out how many opportunities you need to reach your sales target. This helps make your sales predictable.

Here’s a simple example. I’ve used 30% as a starting point; use your own figures if you know them.

Monthly sales revenue target: £10,000
Average sale value: £2,500
Sales needed: 4

If 30% of your meetings become sales, you’ll need 14 meetings to make at least four sales.

If 30% of your leads become meetings, you’ll need 47 leads to generate those meetings.

Then work backwards through each source of leads. How many direct messages, introductions or marketing enquiries do you need to generate 47 leads?

If you know your actual conversion rates, use them. If you don’t, 30% gives you a starting assumption. Track what happens, then update the figures as you learn more about your own sales process.

What is growth strategy?

In simple terms: a clear plan for how your business grows — and can handle growing.

Most owners I work with want more sales. Fewer have a plan for what happens after the sales come in: who does the extra work, which process breaks first, and what it costs to keep up.

More sales alone is not growth. Growth is knowing what to fix first, what to build next, and what to stop doing.

A growth strategy looks at four things:

How the business runs today — are the operations, the team, and the processes ready for more volume, or are they already stretched?

Where growth gets stuck — where are the bottlenecks, the owner dependence, and the manual work that will not scale?

What the market actually wants — who are the right customers, and what do they need next?

What to do first — in priority order, with the value impact.

What you get is a plan you can act on: operational analysis, market research, strategic planning, and execution support. Not a report that sits on a shelf.

Why it matters:

For a growing company, it shows where to fix things before growth makes the problems bigger.

For a company preparing for funding, it shows a lender or investor that growth is planned, not hoped for — and a lender-ready business plan, including financial forecasts, is built on that same plan.

For a seller, a business that can grow without the owner is worth more.

Growth strategy does not tell you to work harder. It tells you where the business needs to change so growth makes it stronger, not just bigger.

AI productivity gains look like a clear win.

Organizations invest in AI, employees adopt it and experience individual productivity gains. 

Yet the expected business benefits don’t always materialize because processes, roles and ways of working remain unchanged.

In this example, a customer service team uses AI to draft responses, saving employees approximately 30 minutes per day.

However, customer response times haven’t improved because the same approval steps remain and the time saved is absorbed by other administrative activities.

The change manager can help identify these barriers, facilitate discussions with business owners about reviewing approval requirements and redirecting capacity, and support employees in adopting the revised ways of working.

Four ways they can contribute:

IDENTIFY THE GAINS: Understand where AI is improving individual productivity and what evidence supports those gains.

CHALLENGE THE VALUE ASSUMPTION: Assess whether individual gains are translating into expected business outcomes. If not, identify the organizational barriers.

ENABLE THE ORGANIZATIONAL SHIFT: Facilitate business decisions with business owners, assess the impacts on roles and workflows and support teams through the transition.

TRACK THE BUSINESS OUTCOME: Monitor whether these changes are contributing to the expected business results, alongside AI adoption.

Business owners make the call on the redesign. The change manager makes sure they see what’s blocking the value and that people aren’t left to figure out the new ways of working alone.

AI Is Making Employees Faster. But Is It Making Organizations Smarter?

We are witnessing an extraordinary shift in individual productivity.
Tasks that once took days now take hours. Reports are generated in minutes. Information is more accessible. Analysis is faster. Employees are increasingly capable of accomplishing more with less effort.
But here is the uncomfortable situation:
Is all this individual intelligence translating into greater organizational intelligence?
I don't think so. Not at the pace we might expect. Also, is it cost effective?
Organizations are becoming faster at producing information, but are they becoming better at making decisions?
Employees are completing tasks more efficiently, but are organizations becoming more effective?
We have more insights than ever, but are we translating those insights into better business outcomes?
And perhaps most importantly, are we fundamentally changing how organizations operate, or simply accelerating the way they have always operated?
There is a critical distinction between individual productivity and organizational intelligence.
An organization is not simply the sum of its employees' productivity. Its intelligence lies in how effectively people, processes, technology, and leadership come together to make decisions, adapt, collaborate, and create value.
Making every employee 30% more productive does not automatically make an organization 30% more effective.
We have invested enormously in making technology more intelligent. But have we invested enough in making our organizations capable of benefiting from that intelligence?
My concern is that we may be creating AI-powered employees operating inside pre-AI organizations.
And that could become one of the greatest limitations of the AI revolution.
I believe the next frontier of AI transformation is not simply about deploying better models, more copilots, or increasingly autonomous agents.
It is about building smarter organizations.
Over the coming weeks, I want to explore why individual AI productivity is not automatically translating into organizational intelligence, what is holding us back, and what leaders need to rethink to close this gap.
For now, I would leave you with one question:
Are we making our organizations smarter, or just making the old ways of working faster?

I used to believe better AI models would automatically make us more productive.

I don’t believe that anymore.

The more I examine how AI is being used in organizations, the more I question whether model capability is our biggest productivity constraint.

We have made generating content, analysing information and exploring alternatives dramatically easier.

But we haven't made deciding, prioritizing or executing equally easy.

In fact, AI introduces an interesting problem.

When the cost of generating another alternative becomes almost zero, knowing when to stop becomes increasingly important.

I believe four human capabilities will matter even more as AI improves.
1. Focus: The ability to choose what deserves our attention when exploring almost anything becomes possible.
2. Consistency: The discipline to convert occasional productivity gains into repeatable ways of working.
3. Judgment: The ability to evaluate evidence, challenge recommendations and make decisions rather than continuously generate alternatives.
4. Execution: The ability to turn increasingly abundant information and recommendations into measurable business outcomes.

These capabilities are not new but AI changes their importance because producing something is becoming easier while deciding what deserves to be produced remains difficult.

Better models expand what we can do.

How we think, decide and execute determines how much of that potential becomes value.

A business problem should never end with another meeting and a list of suggestions.

It should lead to clear actions and measurable improvements.

Let's imagine a company experiencing repeated delays in its internal approval process.

Requests are taking too long to move between departments. Employees are following up constantly, and management is struggling to understand where the delays occur.

How could AI help?

Here's a practical workflow:

STEP 1: DESCRIBE THE PROBLEM

Provide AI with an explanation of how the current approval process works.

STEP 2: MAP THE PROCESS

Ask AI to organise the steps, identify handovers and highlight where delays or duplicated activities may occur.

STEP 3: IDENTIFY POTENTIAL BOTTLENECKS

Ask AI to examine the available process information and identify areas requiring further investigation.

STEP 4: EXPLORE IMPROVEMENTS

Ask it to suggest ways to simplify the process, reduce unnecessary handovers and improve communication.

STEP 5: CREATE AN ACTION PLAN

Turn the recommendations into actions, suggested owners, priorities and measures of success.

STEP 6: MONITOR THE RESULTS

Compare performance before and after the changes.

Are approval times improving? Are fewer requests getting stuck? Is the experience better for employees?

One important point: AI can help analyse the process, but it cannot confirm the actual cause of delays without reliable evidence from the business.

This is the difference between using AI to generate ideas and using AI as part of a structured business improvement workflow.

What process in your organisation would benefit from this approach?

Nigeria is moving towards a new regulatory reality: a financial institution can become systemically important without being a bank.
On 10 November, Nigeria’s Senate passed SB. 959 for a third reading, proposing amendments to the Banks and Other Financial Institutions Act (BOFIA) to strengthen the Central Bank of Nigeria’s oversight of major fintech companies and other non-bank financial institutions.
The proposed framework would allow the CBN to designate qualifying operators as Systemically Important Institutions (SIIs).
The implications are substantial.
Designated institutions could face:
• Regular stress testing and data-integrity assessments.
• Enhanced regulatory reporting and supervisory access to operational systems.
• Stronger cybersecurity and technology-risk controls.
• Mandatory operational resilience and corporate governance standards.
• Greater beneficial ownership transparency.
Why does this matter?
Payment platforms, mobile-money operators, digital lenders and switching companies increasingly sit at the centre of financial activity. Their scale and interconnectedness mean that a technology failure, cyber incident or operational disruption could extend beyond one company and affect the wider financial ecosystem.
The regulatory challenge is no longer simply how to license innovation. It is how to supervise infrastructure whose failure could create systemic consequences.
For fintech founders and investors, this could raise the importance of compliance architecture, technology governance, data integrity and operational resilience.
At Core Intelligence™, we believe the next stage of financial innovation requires institutions to understand not only their growth opportunities, but also their systemic exposure.
As fintechs become critical financial infrastructure, should regulatory supervision increasingly depend on their systemic impact rather than whether they hold a traditional banking licence?

Faster payments. Better mobile banking. Seamless onboarding. Open banking APIs. Automated lending.

And something interesting happened.

Instead of competing with every fintech startup, banks started buying them.

Look at these real examples from around the world:

🇺🇸 1. JPMorgan Chase acquired WePay (2017)

🇦🇺 2. National Australia Bank acquired 86 400 (2021)

🇺🇸 3. Goldman Sachs acquired GreenSky (2022)

The objective? Expand its digital consumer lending capabilities.

Interestingly, Goldman Sachs later sold GreenSky as its strategy changed.

🌍 4. Visa acquired Tink (2022)

Visa completed its €1.8 billion acquisition of European open banking platform Tink.

Tink's technology connects thousands of financial institutions through APIs, enabling financial data access and payment services.

Visa isn't technically a bank, but this acquisition demonstrates how valuable fintech infrastructure has become.

So why are established financial institutions buying fintech companies?

Here is how I see it from a software engineering perspective:

→ Speed: Acquiring proven technology can be faster than building from scratch.

→ Innovation: Fintech startups often develop modern, API-first financial infrastructure.

→ Customer experience: Users increasingly expect instant payments, digital onboarding, and seamless financial services.

→ Engineering talent: Acquisitions bring experienced teams who understand financial technology.

→ Competitive advantage: Owning payment infrastructure, data connectivity, or lending technology can create new revenue opportunities.

But acquiring fintech isn't always a guaranteed success. Integration challenges, regulatory requirements, and changing business strategies can make these investments difficult.

Here's what I believe this means for African fintech developers.

The next valuable fintech startup in Africa might not necessarily be another mobile money wallet.

It could be the company building the infrastructure that banks, microfinance institutions, and payment providers need.

Think about:

Payment orchestration APIs. Fraud detection engines. KYC infrastructure. Cross-border settlement systems. Banking-as-a-Service platforms.

Sometimes the biggest opportunity isn't building another bank. It's building the technology that banks will eventually need.

And that raises an interesting question:

Will African banks increasingly acquire local fintech startups, or will they continue building their technology internally?

I'd love to hear your perspective.

FINANCIAL INNOVATION MUST BE MATCHED WITH EFFECTIVE REGULATION AND INTERNAL CONTROL.
On 10 November 2026, the Nigerian Senate passed for third reading a proposed amendment to the Banks and Other Financial Institutions Act (BOFIA), seeking to strengthen the Central Bank of Nigeria's oversight of systemically important fintech companies and other non-bank financial institutions.
This development highlights an important reality: as fintech companies expand their customer base, transaction volumes and interconnectedness with traditional banks, their operational and financial risks can have wider implications for the financial system.
For compliance, risk management and internal control professionals, this raises important considerations:
Regulatory compliance: Financial institutions must remain aligned with evolving regulatory expectations.
Operational resilience: Technology disruptions and operational failures can create risks beyond individual institutions.
Corporate governance: Clear accountability, effective oversight and transparent ownership structures remain essential.
Cybersecurity: Strong technology-risk management and data protection controls are increasingly important.
Risk-based supervision: Institutions should be assessed according to the scale, complexity and potential impact of their activities.
One lesson stands out: innovation should not outpace governance, and business growth should not outgrow the control environment.
A sustainable financial system requires innovation, accountability, effective supervision and strong internal controls.
The future of banking is digital, but the foundation of trust remains good governance and effective risk management.

The B2B Outreach Guide for Claude Is Here

Six stages, from customer fit to a qualified conversation 👇

We've mapped Claude skills to the structured process behind B2B outreach: customer definition, account research, relevant messaging and follow-up.

Here's how Claude approaches B2B outreach:

1/ Frame
Define the ideal customer, sharpen the offer and name the business problem before building a prospect list.

2/ Diagnose
Research the company, map the buyer and connect current priorities with the public signals that make the account worth investigating.

3/ Choose
Compare account fit, weigh the relevance of the signal and prioritise the prospects whose needs match the offer.

4/ Plan
Turn the research into an opener, a follow-up sequence and a clear next action, with the account context carried between stages.

5/ Stress-Test
Check the source facts, the fit and the relevance of the message before the outreach reaches a prospect.

6/ Communicate
Turn the account research into a specific message, prepare the next response from the actual reply and carry that context into a qualified conversation.

The same backbone every time:
Frame. Diagnose. Choose. Plan. Stress-Test. Communicate.
