💡 B2B vs. B2C Sales: Different Approaches, Same Foundation.
In B2C sales, customers often make faster decisions based on personal needs, emotions, and perceived value.
In B2B sales, decisions usually involve multiple stakeholders, longer sales cycles, and a stronger focus on ROI and long-term business value.
But both have one thing in common:
🎯 Great selling starts with understanding, not pitching.
📖 One of the key lessons from SPIN Selling by Neil Rackham is the importance of asking the right questions before presenting a solution.
The SPIN approach focuses on four types of questions:
🔹 Situation: Understand the customer's current situation.
🔹 Problem: Identify their challenges.
🔹 Implication: Explore the impact of those challenges.
🔹 Need-Payoff: Help the customer recognize the value of solving them.
The takeaway?
Don't just sell a product. Understand your customer's needs and deliver real value              ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
الفرق بين مبيعات B2B , B2C : أساليب مختلفة لكن الأساس واحد💡
في مبيعات B2C، العميل غالبًا بياخد قرار الشراء بشكل أسرع، بناءً على احتياجاته الشخصية ومشاعره والقيمة اللي شايفها في المنتج.
أما في مبيعات B2B، فقرار الشراء عادةً بيكون فيه أكتر من صاحب قرار، ودورة بيع أطول، وتركيز أكبر على العائد من الاستثمار (ROI) والقيمة اللي هتعود على الشركة على المدى الطويل.
لكن في الحالتين، فيه مبدأ أساسي مشترك:
🎯 البيع الناجح بيبدأ بفهم احتياج العميل، مش بعرض المنتج.
📖 من أهم الأفكار اللي بيقدمها كتاب SPIN Selling للكاتب Neil Rackham هي أهمية طرح الأسئلة الصحيحة قبل تقديم أي حل.
ومنهج SPIN بيعتمد على 4 أنواع من الأسئلة:
🔹 Situation – الوضع الحالي: افهم وضع العميل واحتياجاته الحالية.
🔹 Problem – المشكلة: حدد التحديات والمشاكل اللي بيواجهها.
🔹 Implication – التأثير: افهم تأثير المشاكل دي على شغله أو احتياجاته.
🔹 Need-Payoff – قيمة الحل: ساعد العميل يدرك الفائدة اللي هيحققها من حل المشكلة.
الخلاصة؟
متخليش هدفك مجرد بيع منتج، لكن افهم احتياج العميل وقدم له حل يحقق قيمة حقيقية.

Where will the opportunities be in the next 10 years?
I spent today at a Sandeep Das Leadership workshop that tackled exactly this question. Sharing my notes.
Three themes will shape the next decade: Digital Transformation, Go-to-Market Strategy and Change Management.
Inside companies, the opportunity sits in four functions:
→ Manufacturing: increasing output and capacity utilization
→ Logistics: last-mile delivery
→ Purchase: vendor development strategy
→ Sales & Marketing: community building
The speaker gave four pillars for capturing it:
Mindset: Strategy is about making complex choices. Saying no matters more than saying yes.
Build your own framework: Off-the-shelf frameworks fail because they are generic and they don’t scale.
Client acquisition and the 5-95 rule: In B2B, 5% is sales and 95% is marketing. Your product has to be remembered at the moment someone is ready to buy.
Brand: Building a brand is the most important of the four.
He also shared two tools I will be using:
→ 2x2 Matrix: plot your options on two axes so the choice, and the no, becomes visible.
→ Golden Pyramid: structure your thinking from the core idea down to execution.
My takeaway: the next decade will reward leaders who choose clearly, build their own playbook and stay visible.
Which of these four pillars is your business weakest on today? Tell me in the comments.

خلينا نفكر فيها...
في الـ B2B ممكن قيمة الـ Deal تكون أكبر، لكن الوصول للصفقة وإغلاقها ممكن ياخد وقت أطول بسبب الـ Sales Cycle والـ Negotiations والـ Approvals.

وفي الـ B2C ممكن توصل لأول عميل بشكل أسرع، لكن ده مش معناه بالضرورة إنك هتحقق Profit أسرع؛ لأن تكلفة اكتساب العملاء وعدد الـ Sales اللي محتاج تحققها ممكن يكونوا أكبر.

فالموضوع مش مين فيهم بيجيب فلوس أسرع بشكل مطلق، لكن أنهي Model مناسب لطبيعة البيزنس نفسه.

وقبل ما تاخد القرار، فيه عوامل محتاج تحطها في اعتبارك:
Market & Customer Demand: هل فيه احتياج حقيقي للخدمة؟ ومين مستعد يدفع مقابلها؟
Revenue Potential: إيه متوسط قيمة الصفقة والـ Profit المتوقع من كل Segment؟
Sales Cycle & Acquisition Cost: محتاج وقت وتكلفة قد إيه علشان تكسب عميل؟
Resources & Long-term Strategy: هل عندك القدرة تشتغل على الاتنين؟ وهل دخول B2C هيخدم خطتك المستقبلية ولا هيسحب تركيزك من الـ Primary Target؟

وده مش معناه إن دخول B2C لو إنت مستهدف B2B قرار غلط، بالعكس، ممكن يكون خطوة ذكية لو فيه توافق بين الخدمة واحتياج السوق، وعندك القدرة تدير الاتنين.

لكن فيه فرق بين إنك تدخل Segment جديد كجزء من خطة مدروسة، وإنك تدخله لمجرد إنك محتاج فلوس بشكل أسرع.

من وجهة نظري، مش لازم تبدأ بالسوق اللي ممكن يدفع أكتر، ولا السوق اللي ممكن تبيع له أسرع، لكن بالسوق اللي عندك فيه فرصة حقيقية تحقق Traction وRevenue من غير ما تفقد اتجاه البيزنس على المدى الطويل.

حابة أسمع رأي الـ Founders والناس اللي اشتغلت على إطلاق Businesses:
لو الـ Business Model بتاعك قائم على B2B، لكن محتاج تحقق Revenue في البداية، هتدخل B2C مؤقتًا؟ ولا تركز على B2B من أول يوم؟ ولا تشتغل على الاتنين مع بعض؟

FROM SALES EXECUTIVE TO STRATEGIC BUSINESS PARTNER: CREATING VALUE BEYOND THE SALE 

In B2B sales, there is a significant difference between simply selling a product or service and becoming a strategic partner to your customers.

A transactional approach focuses mainly on closing the next deal.

A strategic approach focuses on understanding the customer’s business, identifying opportunities and contributing to their long-term success.

I believe this evolution requires four key principles:

 1. UNDERSTAND THE CUSTOMER’S BUSINESS

Go beyond the product or service you sell. Understand your customer’s strategy, challenges, market position and business objectives.

 2. CREATE SOLUTIONS, NOT JUST OFFERS

Connect your products or services to real business needs. Bring ideas, alternatives and solutions that generate measurable value.

 3. BUILD A TRUST-BASED PARTNERSHIP

Be consistent, transparent and reliable. Share knowledge, communicate proactively and demonstrate that your interest goes beyond the immediate transaction.

 4. THINK ABOUT LONG-TERM GROWTH

Identify new opportunities, anticipate future needs and help your customers evolve. Sustainable business growth should create value for both sides.

In International B2B Sales, this mindset is particularly important. Different markets, cultures and business environments require adaptability, knowledge and a long-term perspective.

The strongest commercial relationships are not built around a single transaction. They are built around shared objectives and mutual success.

The best sales professionals don’t just sell to their customers. They become partners in their growth.

قسمت دوم: فروش سازمانی (B2B Sales)

فروش سازمانی چیست؟

فروش سازمانی (Business to Business) به فرآیندی گفته می‌شود که در آن یک شرکت، محصولات یا خدمات خود را به شرکت یا سازمان دیگری عرضه می‌کند.

در این مدل فروش، برخلاف فروش مستقیم به مصرف‌کننده نهایی، تصمیم‌گیری معمولاً توسط چند نفر از مدیران یا افراد تأثیرگذار در سازمان انجام می‌شود.

ویژگی‌های اصلی فروش B2B

۱. فرآیند تصمیم‌گیری چندمرحله‌ای: تصمیم خرید معمولاً نیازمند بررسی و تأیید چند واحد سازمانی است.

۲. مذاکره تخصصی: قیمت، شرایط پرداخت، کیفیت و تعهدات تأمین‌کننده اهمیت زیادی دارند.

۳. چرخه فروش طولانی‌تر: تبدیل یک فرصت تجاری به قرارداد ممکن است زمان‌بر باشد.

۴. رابطه بلندمدت: حفظ مشتری و ایجاد همکاری مستمر از اهداف مهم این نوع فروش است.

۵. ارزش قرارداد بالاتر: بسیاری از معاملات سازمانی در حجم و مبالغ قابل‌توجه انجام می‌شوند.

مثال‌هایی از فروش سازمانی

- فروش تجهیزات پزشکی به بیمارستان‌ها و مراکز درمانی
- تأمین مواد اولیه کارخانه‌ها
- فروش محصولات غذایی به هتل‌ها و رستوران‌ها
- ارائه نرم‌افزارهای سازمانی به شرکت‌ها

چه چیزی فروش B2B را موفق می‌کند؟

شناخت دقیق کسب‌وکار مشتری، توانایی مذاکره، ارائه راهکار متناسب با نیاز سازمان و ایجاد اعتماد بلندمدت.

در فروش سازمانی، هدف فقط فروش یک محصول نیست؛ بلکه ایجاد یک رابطه تجاری پایدار و سودآور است.

B2B Buyers Use Multiple Channels. Is Your GTM Strategy Connected?
 
Your B2B customers don't follow a perfectly predictable buying journey.
 
They might discover your brand through LinkedIn, explore your website, read a case study, receive an email, attend a webinar, and speak with your sales team.
 
But here's the challenge:

What happens when these touchpoints operate independently?

●     Marketing doesn't know which accounts sales is targeting.

●     Sales lacks visibility into previous customer engagement.

●     Customer data is scattered across platforms.

●     Attribution becomes difficult.

●     Prospects receive disconnected communication.

And the importance of connecting these touchpoints is backed by research.
 
𝗔𝗰𝗰𝗼𝗿𝗱𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝘁𝗼 𝗠𝗰𝗞𝗶𝗻𝘀𝗲𝘆'𝘀 𝟮𝟬𝟮𝟲 𝗚𝗹𝗼𝗯𝗮𝗹 𝗕𝟮𝗕 𝗣𝘂𝗹𝘀𝗲 𝗦𝘂𝗿𝘃𝗲𝘆, 𝗕𝟮𝗕 𝗯𝘂𝘆𝗲𝗿𝘀 𝘂𝘀𝗲 𝗮𝗻 𝗮𝘃𝗲𝗿𝗮𝗴𝗲 𝗼𝗳 𝟭𝟬 𝗰𝗵𝗮𝗻𝗻𝗲𝗹𝘀 𝘁𝗵𝗿𝗼𝘂𝗴𝗵𝗼𝘂𝘁 𝘁𝗵𝗲𝗶𝗿 𝗽𝘂𝗿𝗰𝗵𝗮𝘀𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝗷𝗼𝘂𝗿𝗻𝗲𝘆. More than half of respondents also say they are likely to switch suppliers if they don't receive a seamless experience across channels.
 
This means simply being present on multiple platforms isn't enough. Businesses need to connect every interaction.
 
A stronger GTM strategy requires:

“Be more strategic” is feedback in a trench coat. Underneath, it’s 1 of 3 complaints all dressed up.

 💸 “I can’t see how this connects to revenue.”
Translation: your updates read like an activity log. Posts, opens, events, more posts. Lead with the business goal, then the 1 or 2 things marketing did to move it.

 🎯 “I don’t know what you’d stop doing.”
Translation: you said yes to everything, so nothing looks like a priority. Name what you’re not doing this quarter, and why. In writing.

 😠 “I’m hearing about problems from sales before I hear them from you.”
Translation: bad news is traveling faster than you are. Bring it first, with a fix attached.

Can’t tell which one you got? Ask: “Can you give me an example of something I did that felt strategic, and something that didn’t?”

Then watch them think about it. Most CEOs can answer. And once you know which complaint it was, the fix is a lot smaller than the feedback made it sound.

Which of the 3 have you been handed recently?

Content volume does not compensate for weak positioning.

We frequently audit brands publishing 20–30 times a month who still struggle with inbound pipeline. When we look under the hood, the friction is almost never the creative.

It's the offer.

Consider two agencies competing for the same market:

Agency A (Vague):
"We provide end-to-end digital marketing and growth solutions for modern businesses."
→ Forces the buyer to guess how you solve their immediate problem.
→ Attracts low-budget, high-maintenance prospects.

Agency B (Specific):
"We help B2B SaaS companies generate 10–15 qualified demo calls per month via cold outbound systems."
→ Clarifies the exact ICP, mechanism, and commercial outcome.
→ Commands pricing leverage and shorter sales cycles.

Before increasing your posting frequency this quarter, audit your core proposition:

Can a prospect explain what you do in one sentence?
Is the commercial outcome quantified?
Does it solve one distinct, painful problem?
Amplify clarity, not noise.

Before next year's budget is finalized, examine these two numbers:

The percentage of bookings coming from your current customers.
The share of your marketing spend dedicated to growing those accounts. 

For most B2B companies, there will be a huge gap between these two figures.
Most B2B businesses see large shares of their bookings come from upsells and cross-sells, driven by deeper relationships with current customers. 

But most dollars spent on marketing still go toward pursuing new logos. 

Why? 

Because it is easy for marketing leaders to measure new-logo pipeline. It is also easy for them to communicate this success to the C-Suite and/or board. 

So after a deal closes, that customer account is frequently transferred over to the responsible customer success team. 

Marketing is no longer measured on what happens next: adoption, retention, cross-sells, or upsells. So the budget naturally follows the metrics marketing is held accountable for.

This results in two expensive blind spots:

The part of the business producing some of the most consistent growth gets little support from marketing.

Marketing receives little or no credit when it contributes to expansion revenue.

No one is saying spend should match bookings dollar for dollar. Winning a new customer will always cost more than growing an existing one.

But if your budget is wildly out of proportion to where your revenue actually comes from, it may be time to add an expansion metric to marketing’s scorecard.

Posting once a week and wondering why nobody sees you is like turning your shop lights on one day a month.

In B2B and B2C marketing alike, sporadic visibility destroys momentum.

• Algorithms favor habitual creators
• Audiences require repeated touchpoints to build trust
• Inconsistency communicates a lack of reliability

Are you showing up daily for your target audience, or are you keeping your business in the dark?

Some of the most remarkable investment successes begin long before the rest of the world starts paying attention.

According to a recent Financial Times report, Anthropic's upcoming IPO could generate more than $100 billion in gains for a group of early investors, including several relatively low-profile venture capital firms.

What interests me most isn't the extraordinary amount of wealth being created, but the decisions these investors made when the outcome was far less certain.

It's easy to recognize a successful business in hindsight. Identifying its potential before the market fully appreciates it requires a different combination of knowledge, judgment, patience, and willingness to accept uncertainty.

Of course, for every highly successful venture capital investment, there are many others that never deliver the expected returns.

That's why I believe we should appreciate the discipline behind successful investing rather than simply admire the financial rewards.

There's also an important distinction between having the courage to invest early and blindly pursuing the next popular trend.

Long-term conviction needs to be supported by research, realistic expectations, and responsible risk management.

While Anthropic's IPO represents a remarkable financial opportunity for its early backers, I hope the broader development of artificial intelligence creates value beyond Silicon Valley and the investment community.

The greatest achievement would be seeing that innovation translate into better healthcare, more productive businesses, accessible education, and meaningful opportunities for ordinary people.

Financial rewards are worth celebrating, but the lasting value of innovation should ultimately be measured by what it contributes to society.

The wrong investor costs more than time.

I've seen founders change their narrative based on investor feedback.

The best fundraises don't start with more meetings.

Not every investor is a fit. And that's okay.

The goal isn't more conversations. It's more conversations with investors who can actually say yes.

SA Venture Capital and Private Equity Association (SAVCA)’s 2026 Venture Capital Industry Survey (2025 calendar year) shows capital concentrating:

👉 R2.48bn allocated across 212 deals, versus 222 in 2024
👉 Those deals reached 91 companies, down from 110
👉 Average of 2.3 rounds per funded company

Managers are reserving for and supporting existing positions rather than widening the portfolio. For LPs, that makes reserve strategy and follow-on discipline central to manager selection.

The exits are where this survey earns its weight. Ten exits were reported in 2025, six of them profitable. Those six returned R281.2m on R99.3m invested, roughly 2.8x. That multiple covers the profitable exits only. It is not a cohort-wide return, and ten exits is too small a sample to treat as a trend. But after a long wait for realisations in this market, it is a data point LPs should note.

Three questions we would put to any manager in this environment:
1. What governs the decision to reinvest, and how is that separated from the original investment case?
2. Is the route to exit defined at entry, or assumed at exit?
3. How much of reported performance has been returned to LPs?

These questions apply across private capital in South Africa. At RH Managers, they shape how we have invested in healthcare infrastructure for 12 years, through a financial, operational and ESG due diligence framework applied before capital is committed.

Concentration without rigour compounds risk, with it, compounds returns. 

Source: SAVCA 2026 Venture Capital Industry Survey

Before adding private market exposure, we believe investors should identify which money they may need back soon.

That question helps define its place in a portfolio.

The ARK Venture Fund (ARKVX) is an actively managed closed end interval fund investing in private and public companies relevant to disruptive innovation.

In our view, its potential role is within the portion of a portfolio intended for long term growth.

The rest of the portfolio still needs to support spending, emergencies, and other commitments.

ARKVX shares are not listed on an exchange. Access to invested capital is limited and governed by the Fund’s repurchase policy.

We believe that structure makes liquidity planning part of the allocation decision.

Investors should also consider whether their existing investments already carry similar technology and business risks.

Adding private companies changes the opportunity set. It does not automatically remove overlapping exposures.

In our view, the allocation should fit both the investment goal and the investor’s ability to leave capital invested.

Three mistakes businesses make when implementing AI  and how to avoid them.

AI adoption is growing, but adopting AI tools without a clear implementation strategy can create inefficiencies rather than solve them.
Here are three mistakes businesses should pay attention to:
1. Starting with the tool instead of the problem.
Not every business challenge requires an AI solution. Start by identifying a repetitive task, operational bottleneck or genuine business problem. Then determine whether AI is the right solution.
2. Feeding AI disorganised or incomplete information.
The quality of AI-generated results depends significantly on the quality of the information and instructions provided. Poor inputs can lead to inaccurate or inconsistent outputs.
3. Removing human oversight.
AI can assist with communication, content creation and business processes, but important outputs should still be reviewed. Automation should support human decision-making, not eliminate accountability.
A better approach:
Identify one real business problem.
Organise and validate your information.
Build a relevant AI workflow.
Maintain human review and accountability.
AI implementation is not simply about having the latest tools. It's about using the right tools to solve the right problems.

Brian Tracy: The Fundamentals of Selling Never Go Out of Style

The sales profession lost one of its most influential voices with the passing of Brian Tracy.

Throughout his career, Tracy taught generations of sales professionals the importance of preparation, discipline, goal setting, personal development, and understanding the customer.

His books, including The Psychology of Selling and Eat That Frog!, belong in any serious sales professional’s library.

One of the things I’ve always appreciated about sales is that no matter how many years you’ve spent in the profession, there’s always something more to learn.

Experience is valuable. But so is the willingness to revisit the fundamentals.

That’s a philosophy I believe strongly in, and one that influences how we’re building MWA Consultants.

Technology has changed the sales profession dramatically. We have sophisticated CRM platforms, automation, artificial intelligence, and more customer information available than ever before.

But technology doesn’t eliminate the need for preparation, meaningful conversations, active listening, consistent follow-up, and earning someone’s trust.

Those principles are at the heart of professional sales development.

At MWA Consultants, we believe that successful business development isn’t simply about making more calls or generating more leads.

It’s about creating a disciplined process that identifies opportunities, develops relationships, and helps businesses turn meaningful conversations into measurable results.

Brian Tracy spent his career teaching the importance of mastering the fundamentals and continually improving.

Those lessons remain just as relevant today as they were decades ago.

The tools will continue to change. The fundamentals of professional selling never go out of style.

Rest in peace, Brian Tracy. Your influence on the sales profession will continue for generations.

#BrianTracy #SalesDevelopment #SalesLeadership #BusinessDevelopment #MWAConsultants

We often find ourselves pulled in two directions. We want the freedom to experiment, learn and try new ideas, but we also need to deliver reliably and keep up with the goals in front of us.
It can be tempting to choose one side over the other. When the focus stays only on new ideas, they may never turn into something real, and when it stays only on delivery, the team can gradually lose the space it needs to learn and grow. Innovation really depends on both.
This is the paradox of innovation. Exploration and delivery compete for the same time, attention and resources, yet each relies on the other to create lasting value. The challenge is not to resolve this tension but to keep working with it as priorities shift.

I'd love to hear how it looks from your side. Does your team tend to lean more towards exploring or towards delivering?

What can a two-person company in Tokyo build with an AI team? 🤔
 
Quite a lot. My Columbia Business School students just heard how.
 
I met Philippe Gralll at Thinkers50 in London. 

He’s an executive coach to CEOs across industries including luxury, retail and pharma, and we’re both in Marshall Goldsmith’s #100Coaches community. 

So, I invited him to talk to my class about working in the age of AI.
 
His message: AI is the fastest way to scale yourself, your team, or your startup. But the tools are just the tip of the iceberg.
 
Underneath:

 👉 Mindset: your why, the part AI can’t replace

 👉 System: how you structure, teach and operate your AI

 👉 Technology: one brain, specialist hands
 
The leadership lessons I took from it:

 🔷 Stay curious. The leaders who win ask “what if?” before “what’s the risk?”

 🔷 Learn by doing. You can’t read your way into AI fluency.

 🔷 Start small. Run a pilot, not a transformation program.

 🔷 Fail fast. Trial and error is the strategy, not the detour.

 🔷 Share your learning. Every experiment teaches more when others see it.

 🔷 Stay open-minded. The best use case may not be the one you planned.
 
The students got it. They didn’t ask which tool to buy. They asked what to hand over, what to keep, where to start, and how to keep learning. That’s the right instinct.
 
Thank you, Philippe Grall, for the generosity and the clarity. And thank you, Thinkers50, for creating the event where we met.
 
What’s one small pilot you’ll run with AI this week? 👇

Some of the best business lessons I ever learned came from a smoothie company.

So many old innocent drinks faces popped up on my B Corp news last week, and it got me thinking about how much of Happity was shaped by my time there.

There’s one picture from the wall at innocent I’ve never forgotten. (Some of you will know exactly the one I mean.)

A head, surrounded by speech bubbles all saying “no”. And inside the head, one big bubble saying “yes”.

I didn’t know then how much I’d need it.

When you build something in a sector people don’t understand, you hear “no” a lot:

“Baby classes aren’t a big enough market.”
“You can’t build a business with a fully remote team of parents.”
“You’ll need a man on the founding team to get investment.” (Yes, someone really said that.)

But if you believe in something strongly enough, the “yes” in your own head has to be louder than all of them.

Today Happity is the UK’s largest platform for baby and toddler classes, and a Certified B Corp, just like the company that taught me that lesson.

And innocent has never quite left me. I still have my Golden Bottle and my “Services to Fruit” award. I borrowed the rosette idea for Happity (you can spot it in the photo). We run our own version of the MMM, with a wellness moment (instead of crazy random activities - pretending to be a firework anyone?!) at the end. I even have a grass floor in my office. 🌱

So, innocent alumni: what do you still carry with you from your time there?
And for everyone else: what’s the “no” you’re glad you ignored?

This week my professor asked me to interview a finance leader in front of our class, with no warning. 😅 I was scared at first. By the end, I loved it.

Here’s what I learnt from Cyrous Jamé, who leads finance teams at Pantheon and mentored start-up teams in our class at UC Berkeley Sutardja Center for Entrepreneurship and Technology (SCET).

📅 Picture a big Q4 target landing on your team with 53 days to go. The usual reflex is a heroic sprint and late nights. Not for Cyrous.

➡️ 𝟭% 𝗯𝗲𝘁𝘁𝗲𝗿 𝗲𝘃𝗲𝗿𝘆 𝗱𝗮𝘆: he asks each person to improve the one piece they work on. In less than a year, 1% a day can change your mindset and workflow.

➡️ Curiosity first: it’s the trait he looks for in an interview and in his colleagues.

➡️ Think 𝟱 𝘆𝗲𝗮𝗿𝘀 𝗮𝗵𝗲𝗮𝗱: imagine what could happen in five years to decide what you build today. He manages the same way: participative management (deciding with his team, not for them), collaboration, and a real appetite for risk.

That’s my lesson: big goals come from small daily changes, made by curious people who look five years ahead.

Interviewing him was challenging, and it showed me a side of my personality I didn’t know.

🙏 Thank you Cyrous Jamé, for answering every question so openly, and Victoria Howell for inviting him to class (and for putting me on the spot).

Sales is not just about selling. It is about understanding people.

I have always believed that the true art of sales lies in building relationships. And, perhaps, this is also the most challenging part of our profession.

Every day, we interact with different companies, meet people with different personalities, expectations, perspectives and business goals. Each conversation requires a different approach. We need to listen, understand, build trust and find common ground.

There is no universal formula for building relationships. Knowing your product and being a good negotiator are important, but they are not enough. You need emotional intelligence, genuine interest in people and the ability to inspire confidence.

Because people don’t simply buy products or services. They buy experiences, trust, value and most importantly, the people behind them.

So, don’t just sell. Connect. Inspire. Create value. Build relationships that last.

Because the strongest sales strategy will always begin with a genuine human connection.

🔥🔆Leadership 2.0: Why Great Leadership Starts with Emotional Intelligence🔆🔥

In today's fast-changing workplace, technical expertise and professional experience are important, but they are not enough to make someone an effective leader.

Great leadership requires more than managing tasks and delivering results. It requires the ability to adapt to change, understand people, manage emotions, and inspire others.

This is one of my key takeaways from Leadership 2.0 by Travis Bradberry and Jean Greaves, authors of Emotional Intelligence 2.0.

The book highlights the importance of combining Adaptive Leadership with Emotional Intelligence (EQ) to become a more effective leader.

Here are five lessons that particularly stood out to me:

1️⃣ Adaptive Leadership

Great leaders don't resist change, they embrace it. They remain flexible, open to learning, and capable of guiding their teams through uncertainty.

2️⃣ Self-Awareness

Effective leadership starts with knowing yourself. Understanding your emotions, strengths, weaknesses, and how your behavior affects others is essential.

3️⃣ Self-Management

Knowing how you feel is one thing, managing how you respond is another. Great leaders remain composed under pressure, manage stress, and avoid impulsive reactions.

4️⃣ Social Awareness

Leadership is about people. It requires listening actively, showing empathy, understanding different perspectives, and recognizing the needs of others.

5️⃣ Relationship Management

This is where emotional intelligence translates into leadership impact. Building trust, managing conflicts, developing people, and creating positive relationships are essential to leading successful teams.

My Biggest Takeaway 💡

Leadership is not about a title or position. It is a continuous journey of self-awareness, learning, and adaptation.

The best leaders are not necessarily those who have all the answers, but those who understand themselves, connect with others, and bring out the best in their teams.

‼️Ultimately, before you can effectively lead others, you must first learn to lead yourself.

Stop Trying to Book the Meeting. Start Earning It.

I came across a sales training post this morning outlining five discovery questions designed to help salespeople book more meetings.

Good questions, actually.

Understand the customer’s situation. Identify their problems. Explore the implications. Then ask for the meeting.

Nothing fundamentally wrong with that approach.

But I think we’re missing something important.

The objective of discovery shouldn’t be to book a meeting. It should be to determine whether there’s a good reason to have one.

Those are two very different things.

Over the years, I’ve watched salespeople become so focused on advancing an opportunity that they forget to establish whether an opportunity actually exists.

They ask questions designed to uncover pain.

And when the customer says everything is working fine, they keep digging.

Surely something must be wrong.

Surely there’s a problem hiding somewhere.

Surely if we ask the right question, we’ll find something we can sell them.

Maybe.

Or maybe the customer is telling you the truth.

Here’s a concept that shouldn’t be revolutionary.

Not everyone needs what you’re selling.

And that’s perfectly fine.

One of the most valuable skills a salesperson can develop is recognizing the difference between a customer who has a problem worth solving and someone who simply agreed to answer a few questions.

I’ve spent much of my career in complex sales environments, including enterprise technology, where relationships and credibility often matter considerably more than the immediate transaction.

And I’ve learned something.

Sometimes the most productive sales conversation ends with you telling the customer that you don’t think they need your product.

Imagine that.

A salesperson who actually recommends against making a purchase.

You might lose a transaction.

But you could gain something considerably more valuable.

Trust.

And trust has a funny way of generating opportunities that no discovery script could ever anticipate.

Now, don’t misunderstand me.

I believe in disciplined sales processes. I believe in asking thoughtful questions. And I absolutely believe in understanding the financial and operational implications of a customer’s challenges.

But there’s a difference between genuine curiosity and a rehearsed interrogation designed to manufacture urgency.

Customers can usually tell which one they’re experiencing.

The best salespeople don’t just know when to ask for the meeting. They know when not to.

Because the objective isn’t to fill your calendar.

It’s to build relationships that eventually fill your pipeline.

And there’s a world of difference.

Here’s my question for sales leaders: Are we teaching our teams how to discover opportunities, or simply how to manufacture appointments?

That is where the real opportunity lies.

I’m excited to share some of the business books I’ve read so far 📚. Each book has given me a new perspective on business and personal growth, and I’d like to share some of the core lessons that have stuck with me from each one.

The Lean Startup by Eric Ries: This book taught me that you don't need to have everything figured out before starting. Testing an MVP can save you time and money on ideas that might not work. The core principle is simple: build, measure, and learn.

The $100 Startup by Chris Guillebeau: The idea I loved most from this book is that you don't need a huge budget to start a business. This book provides a framework for building a business focused on creating value and solving real problems.

The 4-Hour Workweek by Tim Ferriss: Being busy can be a form of laziness. Staying occupied doesn't always mean being productive. By eliminating or delegating unnecessary tasks and focusing on your Most Important Tasks (MITs), you can achieve much more.

The Personal MBA by Josh Kaufman: A book that covers key aspects of business, including value creation, finance, sales, marketing, value delivery, psychology, leadership, and much more. It offers practical ideas that challenge the way you think about business.

This Is Marketing by Seth Godin: The key idea I took away is that marketing isn't just about selling; it's about understanding people and creating something that genuinely matters to them.

How to Win Friends and Influence People by Dale Carnegie: This was one of the first books I read. One lesson that stuck with me is that listening, understanding others, and showing genuine interest can be far more powerful than simply trying to convince them.

We Have a Deal by Natalie Reynolds: This book taught me to approach negotiation differently, recognize common negotiation mistakes, ask better questions, and handle objections effectively.

I'm still learning, and there's a lot more to read. Every book on this list has been worth my time. One thing I've realized is that reading is only the first step. The real value comes from applying what you learn.

✅ Empowerment: Give employees the confidence, responsibility and opportunity to make decisions, take initiative and contribute meaningfully.

✅ Accountability: Establish clear expectations, monitor performance fairly and encourage ownership of individual and team results.

After 15 years of building RecruitMe Plus, the best sales strategy I've ever used is one I'll never change.

HONESTY

I've read about sales techniques
Negotiation tactics
Buyer psychology
How to identify pain points
How to create urgency
How to handle objections
Some people even recommend bluffing

But the strategy that's worked best for me has always been much simpler:
Tell the truth!

If we can deliver something, I say we can
If we can't, I say we can't

If a client's expectations are unrealistic, I tell them

If the salary won't attract the talent they want, I tell them

If I don't believe we can successfully close a search, I'd rather walk away than sell a promise my team can't keep

Does that mean I win every deal?
Of course not.

I've probably lost business because of it.

But I've also built client relationships that lasted for years!

Because once expectations are clearly set, something important happens:
Trust replaces selling
You don't need to constantly manage disappointment
You don't need to explain promises you shouldn't have made
You don't need to remember what you told someone during the sales process

You simply deliver what you said you would.

After 15 years, I've learned that the best sales strategy isn't always the cleverest one

Sometimes it's simply:
Never sell something you don't believe you can deliver.

It may cost you a deal today, but trust me, it can win you a client for years.

🚀 7 STRATEGIES TO EXPAND YOUR BUSINESS INTO NEW MARKETS

Business growth isn't just about selling more products or services. It's about identifying new opportunities, reaching the right customers, building strong relationships, and expanding your market presence.

If you're planning to take your business to the next level, here are 7 powerful strategies to successfully enter new markets.

1️⃣ Conduct In-Depth Market Research
Understand your target audience, customer behavior, market demand, competitors, industry trends, and potential business opportunities before entering a new market.

2️⃣ Identify the Right Target Audience
Define your ideal customer profile (ICP). Understand customer pain points, purchasing behavior, demographics, and expectations to build an effective customer acquisition strategy.

3️⃣ Develop a Strong Market Entry Strategy
Choose the right approach, whether it's direct sales, strategic partnerships, franchising, distribution networks, or digital expansion.

4️⃣ Build Strategic Business Partnerships
Connect with local businesses, distributors, industry experts, and potential partners. Strong business relationships can accelerate market penetration and brand awareness.

5️⃣ Adapt Your Products and Marketing Strategy
Every market is different. Customize your products, pricing strategy, branding, and marketing campaigns according to local customer needs and market preferences.

6️⃣ Leverage Digital Marketing and Technology
Use SEO, content marketing, social media marketing, LinkedIn marketing, email marketing, and targeted advertising to increase brand visibility and generate qualified leads.

7️⃣ Monitor Performance and Scale Strategically
Track KPIs such as customer acquisition cost (CAC), conversion rates, revenue growth, customer retention, and market share. Analyze results and continuously optimize your business growth strategy.

💡 Remember: Successful market expansion doesn't happen overnight. It requires proper planning, market intelligence, customer understanding, consistent execution, and long-term relationship building.

More traffic! More clicks! More ad spend! If it continues, your website might need a bigger door just to let everyone in. 😅

My unpopular opinion: more visitors don't automatically mean more revenue.
Before spending more to bring people in, you should think: How much more could your business earn from the traffic you're already paying for?

That's where Conversion Rate Optimization (CRO) becomes an important part of the growth strategy.

CRO isn't just about increasing the percentage of visitors who buy, but about identifying friction across the customer journey, running experiments, and measuring whether those changes greatly improve business outcomes.

For example, take our work with Karma & Luck:

We identified opportunities across three areas:
→ Product discovery: Helping customers find products more easily.
→ Site speed: Addressing friction that could interrupt the shopping experience.
→ Bundle purchasing: Improving the experience to encourage bigger baskets.

After experimentation, the results were significant:
📈 Conversion rate: 1.20% → 1.95% (+62.5%)
🛒 Average order value: $120 → $170 (+41.7%)
💰 Revenue per visitor: $1.44 → $3.32 (+130%)

Now, consider what that could mean at scale.

With 100,000 visitors, the presentation models revenue increasing from $144,000 to $331,500 - an additional $187,500 without increasing traffic.

That's the potential of improving both how many visitors convert and how much they spend.
The opportunity isn't limited to e-commerce. A SaaS business might focus on trial-to-paid conversion or qualified pipeline. A travel company might optimize completed bookings and booking revenue. The right metrics depend on the business model and its goals.

More acquisition can help you grow, but testing, learning from customer behavior, and implementing winning experiments can help you get more value from the demand you've already created.

2️⃣ Understand Your Users
Know who experiences the problem, how they solve it today, and what's missing.

3️⃣ Validate Before You Build
Talk to potential customers. Test your assumptions. Make sure people actually need your solution.

4️⃣ Build Around the Problem
Start with the core functionality that solves the biggest pain point. Add features as users grow.

Think about it:
Problem → User Research → MVP → Feedback → Scalable SaaS Product.

The best SaaS products aren't necessarily the ones with the most features.

They're the ones that solve a problem so well that customers don't want to go back to their old way of working.

🌎 GLOBAL BANKING INTELLIGENCE | LATIN AMERICA

From National Payment Systems to Regional Financial Interoperability

Latin America's banking transformation is driven by instant payments, digital banking, fintech innovation and regional cooperation.

① INSTANT PAYMENT INFRASTRUCTURE

🇧🇷 Brazil: #Pix
🇲🇽 Mexico: SPEI, CoDi, DiMo
🇨🇴 Colombia: Bre-B
🇦🇷 Argentina: Transferencias 3.0
🇨🇱 Chile: TEF
🇵🇪 Peru: Yape, Plin
🇨🇷 Costa Rica: SINPE Móvil
🇵🇾 Paraguay: SIPAP

These systems are transforming domestic payments. The next challenge is cross-border interoperability.

② BANKING & FINTECH ECOSYSTEM

Leading banking groups:
• Brazil: Itaú Unibanco, Banco do Brasil, Banco Bradesco
• Mexico: BBVA en México, Banorte, Santander México
• Colombia: Bancolombia, Banco Davivienda
• Chile: Banco de Chile, BancoEstado
• Argentina: Galicia Bank, Banco Macro

Digital challengers and fintech platforms:
• Nubank, Mercado Pago, dLocal, Ualá, Nequi, Yape and Clip.

Open Finance, APIs, digital wallets, neobanks and fintech-bank partnerships are reshaping competition, customer experience and financial inclusion.

③ REGIONAL PAYMENT CONNECTIVITY

PROJECT LÚMINA, led by the Latin American Reserve Fund (FLAR), involves the central banks of Chile, Colombia, Paraguay, Peru and Uruguay. Supported by GFTN and MIRA, with Nexus Global Payments as technical partner, it explores linking domestic instant payment systems through the Nexus model. Readiness assessments and a shared roadmap are underway. It is not yet operational.

④ INSTITUTIONAL ECOSYSTEM

• FLAR: Regional financial stability and reserve support.
• Inter-American Development Bank: Development financing and digital financial infrastructure.
• CAF -banco de desarrollo de América Latina y el Caribe- : Regional development and economic integration.
• CEMLA: Central bank cooperation and monetary research.
• FEDERACIÓN LATINOAMERICANA DE BANCOS - FELABAN: Latin American banking sector representation.
• ASBA- Association of Supervisors of Banks of the Americas: Banking supervision and regulatory cooperation.
• BIS - Bank of international settlements : Global financial infrastructure, standards and Nexus origins.
• MERCOSUR: Regional economic and trade integration.
• Global Finance & Technology Network (GFTN): Financial technology collaboration.
• Nexus Global Payments: Cross-border instant payment connectivity.

⑤ EMERGING FINANCIAL INTELLIGENCE

AI-driven banking, open finance, digital identity, tokenisation, CBDCs, stablecoins, cybersecurity, AML/CFT and data governance are shaping the next phase.

THE BIGGER PICTURE →

Fragmented infrastructure, currency differences, remittance costs and regulatory divergence make regional interoperability a strategic priority.

Connecting national payment systems and financial institutions could unlock a more integrated regional ecosystem.

The next frontier is regional financial intelligence and connectivity.

Introducing FlexPay – Earned Wage Access Platform!
What if employees could access a portion of the salary they have already earned, even before the regular payday?
Our MBA capstone project explores the “payday gap” faced by salaried employees when urgent expenses arise before salary day.
FlexPay is a proposed employer-linked digital platform that calculates eligible earned wages, enables employees to request a controlled withdrawal and supports settlement through the next payroll cycle.
The concept follows a B2B2C business model connecting employers, employees and payment partners, with a transparent flat service fee of ₹20 per withdrawal.
We have developed a demonstration website to showcase the proposed business model and user journey. The current prototype uses simulated balances and transactions and does not transfer real money.
This project has provided us with an opportunity to explore fintech innovation, employee financial wellness, strategic management and responsible AI applications in payroll operations.
Special thanks to Professor Dr. Pardeep Kumar for his valuable guidance, continuous support and encouragement throughout this project. His insights have helped us shape our ideas and strengthen our understanding of the practical application of business concepts.

The future of payments isn't a choice between traditional banking and new technology.
I think it's increasingly clear that we'll need both.

Yesterday, U.S. Federal Reserve Governor Christopher Waller made an important point about digital finance: new payment technologies will continue to develop, but established financial infrastructure and central bank money will remain essential to trust. That distinction matters.

There's a tendency in fintech to frame innovation as replacing whatever came before it. Banks versus fintechs. Traditional payment networks versus blockchain. Old infrastructure versus new. But financial systems rarely evolve that neatly. The real opportunity is to connect these technologies in ways that improve how money moves without compromising reliability, oversight or customer confidence.

For me, the most interesting companies won't necessarily be those trying to replace the entire financial system. They'll be the ones making its different parts work better together.

Nice to see Clariteer in Trends, De Tijd and La Libre today 😊
 
People often ask me why I started another company after Proxyclick. Part of the answer is simple: it’s a fascinating problem, and I’m lucky to work on it with Gregory Blondeau, Caroline Deuse and Jan-Pieter George. But there’s another reason, and it goes back to my first VC investment.
 
After the sale, I invested into a climate fund through Carbon Equity. Bill Gates’ book on climate had made a big impression on me. Here in Europe, the climate conversation is mostly about consuming less. Gates shows that innovation is an equally powerful lever, with things like low-carbon steel and cement, and I wanted to be part of that.
 
That’s what I like about venture capital. When you buy an existing share on the stock market, your money goes to whoever sold it to you. In a VC fund, your money goes straight into the companies building the future you want to see.
 
And more people can do this now. Europe is pushing hard to open private equity to individual investors (e.g. ELTIF 2.0), because it sees it as a way to fund its own future next to the US and China.
 
Where it gets painful is ... reporting. Private equity is a sophisticated asset class full of very smart people, yet following your positions still looks like it did decades ago. With listed shares you know exactly where you stand, in real time. With PE funds you receive a steady stream of PDFs, and the one number that matters is often hiding in a footnote on page 37 😅
 
Large institutions have analysts for that. Individual investors and small family offices usually don’t, and end up doing it by hand.
 
That’s what we’re working on at Clariteer: turning that pile of PDFs into one clear, up-to-date view of your portfolio, so you can follow performance, see capital calls coming and handle the tax side. In Belgium, with the new capital gains tax, that last part has become a real headache.
 
Thanks to Trends, De Tijd and La Libre for the coverage 🙏

Close to half of VC decision-makers have backed at least one real winner. Only 3% have backed ten.

Blake Jackson and I have assembled what we believe is the largest and most comprehensive dataset of individual U.S. venture capitalists ever built: over 100,000 professionals affiliated with U.S. VC firms between 1996 and 2025, roughly 37,000 of them investment professionals.

We count an investment as “successful” if the startup subsequently went public, reached a unicorn valuation, or was acquired for at least five times the total capital the company had raised.

45% of middle- and senior-level VCs have at least one successful investment. Roughly a coin flip. If your ambition is to be able to say, at the end of your career, that you backed one real winner, the odds are far better than the folklore suggests. And of course the flip side is just as true: a single hit is not evidence of skill. It is close to the base rate.

Everything changes when you ask not whether a VC ever hit, but how often. Among the decision-makers, 45% reach one, 28% reach two, 11% reach five, and 3% reach ten.

Fewer than four hundred people is the entire population of U.S. venture capitalists over three decades credited with ten or more successful investments. It is smaller than the combined partner rosters of a handful of large firms.

There is no number of wins after which the next one becomes easy. When we randomly reassign VCs across deals, the number of VCs with ten or more successful investments declines substantially. This lends further support to the thesis that skill plays a critical role in long-term VC success.

𝗛𝗼𝘄 𝗶𝘀 𝘃𝗲𝗻𝘁𝘂𝗿𝗲 𝗱𝗲𝗮𝗱 𝘄𝗵𝗲𝗻 𝗶𝘁’𝘀 𝗴𝗼𝗻𝗲 𝗺𝗮𝗶𝗻𝘀𝘁𝗿𝗲𝗮𝗺?

Calling venture dead while it’s taking over the entire economy is like looking at an expanding ocean full of ships and declaring it empty because a few of them got bigger.

And when critics of the industry focus only on the concentration of capital – and using a narrow definition of what “counts” as real venture capital – risks missing the bigger picture. The pool of capital, players, and ambition has grown dramatically.

A few days ago, I shared how I ended up deleting all my AI bots. 😊 The post sparked quite a conversation. So, here's the sequel:

The lesson wasn’t that AI doesn’t work. I was using AI built for flying when I was still crawling.

Every business goes through or is in one of the four stages: Crawl. Walk. Run. Fly. AI can help at every stage & also accelerate the evolution but you need to know which stage you are in.

CRAWL: Get the basics right. Understand your product, market and customers. Use AI for research and positioning.
WALK: Know your customer. Use AI to identify opportunities and prepare meaningful conversations.
RUN: You have traction. Use AI to scale outreach, follow-ups and delivery.
FLY: Your processes are mature. Now automation and AI agents can deliver real scale.

My mistake? Jumping straight to fly.

I had the bots, but not all the foundations to make them effective.

The bigger lesson: 

AI adoption isn’t just a technology decision. It’s a business maturity decision.

Experience and judgement tell you where you are. AI can help you get to the next stage faster.

It’s not about using more or less AI. It’s about creating more value with the right AI at the right time.

AI might reduce the time required to build software.

The IT industry isn’t dying. It’s being forced to evolve.

The companies that refuse to change will struggle.

The companies that embrace AI and rethink how they create value could become much stronger.

One thing is certain:

**The future won’t belong to the IT company with the most developers.

It will belong to the company that solves the right problems, in the smartest way.**

Are you preparing your company for an AI-powered future, or are you still selling the same business model you were selling five years ago?

text:
If AI replaces millions of jobs, who will buy what AI produces?

Amazon, Google and other tech companies are already cutting jobs. But let us look beyond technology for a minute.

A person who loses a job still has home loan and car loan EMIs, school fees, household expenses and a family to support.

And the effect does not stop there:

• Real estate demand goes down
• Loan defaults can go up
• Car sales slow down
• Amazon loses customers, Swiggy loses orders
• Restaurants and local shops lose business

The economy runs on purchasing power, not just productivity.

Every company wants to automate to reduce cost. But every company also needs customers who can afford to buy from it.

Please do not get me wrong, I am not against AI. It can solve difficult problems and open up new opportunities. But automation should not become a race to eliminate the very customers who keep the economy running.

The real issue is not how many jobs AI can replace. It is how we grow productivity without killing purchasing power.

I would like to hear from business leaders, founders, economists and tech professionals.

Are we building an economy for AI, or an economy for people powered by AI?

#AI #ArtificialIntelligence #FutureOfWork #IndianEconomy #Automation #Leadership

How to Use AI in HR for 2027 Workforce Planning?

Before finalizing your 2027 Manpower Plan, use your 2026 HR data to identify workforce gaps, forecast future needs, and evaluate organizational effectiveness.

A practical 6-step methodology:

1. Data Collection & Validation

Collect and organize:

- Current Headcount & Job Descriptions.
- Performance Appraisals & KPI Results.
- Turnover & Absenteeism.
- Payroll Cost & Approved Vacancies.

AI Application: Organize data, identify missing information, and detect inconsistencies.

Output: Workforce Data Report.

2. Performance & Productivity Analysis

Analyze employee and departmental performance against business targets.

AI Application: Identify performance trends, productivity gaps, recurring issues, and competency gaps.

Output: Performance Analysis Report.

3. Workforce Gap Analysis

Compare current workforce capabilities with 2027 business requirements.

Identify:

- Critical Positions.
- Required Skills & Competencies.
- Hiring Needs.
- Training & Reskilling Opportunities.

AI Application: Conduct Skills Gap Analysis and identify workforce priorities.

Output: Workforce Gap Matrix.

4. Manpower Forecasting & Scenario Planning

Use business forecasts, workload, current headcount, expected turnover, and budget to build three scenarios:

- Business as Usual.
- Business Expansion.
- Cost Optimization.

AI Application: Compare required headcount, hiring timelines, operational capacity, and manpower costs across scenarios.

Output: 2027 Manpower Plan & Budget Forecast.

5. Organizational Structure Review

Evaluate:

- Span of Control.
- Reporting Lines.
- Role Overlaps.
- Organizational Layers.
- Job Responsibilities.

AI Application: Identify structural gaps, duplicated responsibilities, and opportunities to improve organizational efficiency.

Output: Organizational Structure Assessment.

6. HR Action Plan & Performance Monitoring

Translate findings into an execution plan covering Recruitment, Learning & Development, Succession Planning, Organizational Changes, Budget, and KPIs.

AI Application: Develop implementation timelines and dashboards to monitor Actual vs. Planned Results.

Output: 2027 HR Strategic Action Plan & Monitoring Dashboard.

Final Thought:

AI can analyze data, forecast workforce needs, and support management decisions. But data quality, human judgment, and management accountability remain essential.

Start with Data. Identify the Gaps. Forecast the Needs. Plan for 2027.

Define it — write the one job in one plain line.
Deliver it — do it for one real person, end to end.

Small is not the enemy of big. Unfinished is. A finished small thing teaches you what the big version should be.

Not every AI use case deserves the same level of governance.

A customer-facing recommendation engine and an internal productivity assistant carry very different risk profiles. 

Treating them identically either slows down low-risk work or under-protects high-risk work.

Before approving an AI use case, consider four dimensions:
Data sensitivity: What type of data is processed?

Business impact: What happens if the system makes a wrong decision?

Autonomy: Is AI supporting a human, or making decisions with limited intervention?
Regulatory exposure: Could the use case trigger privacy, sectoral, employment, consumer or other obligations?

Together, these can help determine whether a use case needs a basic review, an enhanced privacy and security assessment, legal and compliance review, executive approval or ongoing monitoring.

The point is not to create bureaucracy around every AI experiment. It is to apply governance proportionately.

Risk-based governance is usually more sustainable than treating every AI application identically.

Save the carousel for your next AI risk assessment.

Which of these four dimensions does your team assess least rigorously?

Here's what that looks like in practice:

1️⃣  MVP mindset: Start small, test fast, kill what doesn't work
2️⃣ Iteration over perfection: Your sequences, your ICP, your hiring profile; all of it should evolve quarterly
3️⃣ Prove ROI or die: If you can't show pipeline impact, you lose headcount. Period.
4️⃣ Build in public: Share what's working with your AEs, your marketing team, your leadership. Transparency builds trust.

The SDR leaders who get promoted aren't the ones running the cleanest dashboards.

They're the ones who build something that scales. Those who take ownership as if it were their company. Who treat every quarter like a funding round.

Your startup doesn't need more employees. It needs better systems.

Over the years, as an entrepreneur and startup mentor, I have seen founders make one common mistake: whenever operations become overwhelming, their first instinct is to hire more people.

But adding people to an unstructured business often creates more confusion, not efficiency.
Missed follow-ups, delayed decisions, repeated mistakes, unclear responsibilities, and constant founder involvement are not always signs of an understaffed team.

They are often signs of missing systems.

Before expanding your team, focus on building four essential systems:
1. Lead Management System: Track every opportunity, customer interaction, and follow-up.
2. Task & Ownership System: Define who is responsible for what, with clear timelines and accountability.
3. Communication System: Establish structured updates so important information doesn't get lost in endless calls and messages.
4. Reporting System: Use measurable data to identify problems and make better decisions.

A business cannot scale sustainably if every small decision requires the founder's approval.

Your role as a founder should gradually shift from managing every task to building processes, developing leaders, and creating accountability.

Hire people to accelerate growth. Build systems to sustain it.

Because the true strength of a startup is not how many people it employs, but how effectively it operates.

Founders, ask yourself: If you step away for a week, will your business continue running smoothly?

One of the greatest business lessons I learned came from watching a customer reinvent itself.

In the early 2000s, we won intermodal business with a company that had been around for more than 30 years.

Despite their history, their leadership team operated with the energy of a startup. They had a bold vision to transform their business, and they took the time to share that vision with us as their transportation partner.

I remember walking away from those conversations genuinely rooting for them.

And then I watched them do exactly what they said they would do.

That experience taught me five lessons I've carried throughout my career:

1. Your history doesn't have to define your future. It's never too late to reinvent yourself.
2. Vision means little without execution. A great plan only matters if you follow through.
3. Great leaders bring others along. They make sure their partners understand the bigger picture.
4. Passion is contagious. Their belief in what they were building made me believe in it, too.
5. Never stop challenging the status quo. Established companies can still think like entrepreneurs.

More than 20 years later, I still follow their success.

They probably never realized how much I learned from them. I was there to help move their freight, but they taught me a lot about leadership.

What's a lesson you learned from a customer that still sticks with you today?

Starting my own venture, I expected to unlearn almost everything I knew.

I was wrong.

After 27+ years in large financial institutions, I only had to unlearn one thing. The rest turned out to be my biggest advantage.

Here’s how those years shaped the way I build a startup: what I kept, what I changed, and how to start.

What I kept:

In large institutions, I learned the value of process and working across teams. Clear SOPs and quick collaboration often improved efficiency.

I still value that discipline as a founder.

What I changed:

A business needs something established institutions rarely did: deciding with less information.

So I listen more closely, and I help the team focus on what matters most.

How to start:

→ Write down the few things that must happen the same way every time
→ Keep each one short enough that people actually read it
→ Review them as you learn
→ Leave room for judgment on the exceptions

Process handles the routine, and it’s your judgment that handles the new.

What’s one process from your past that you still use today?

Leadership isn't just about telling people what to do or getting them fired up.

There's plenty of that on social media already.

Sometimes, it's about having an honest conversation, letting someone make a mistake, and helping them learn from it.

Ward Couillard, Director at Glass Lewis, recently shared a little about his experience working with me.

One of the things he talked about was the importance of relationships, honest conversations, and learning from mistakes.

That's something I've always believed. You don't help people grow by pretending they're never going to get things wrong.

And hearing that some of our conversations have stuck with Ward means a lot.

Ward, I appreciate you taking the time to share this. Thank you, brother.

#LeadershipDevelopment #Coaching #Mentorship #ProfessionalGrowth

The leaders who succeed all have something in common: 

They know which leadership style to use for which moment, and don't get attached to any single one.

What might work in the initial stages of growing a company will be very different to that of a company that's decades deep.

So here are 9 leadership styles, and when to use each one 👇

🔄 Adaptive Leadership

Whitney Wolfe Herd, Founder of Bumble
↳ Adjusts the approach to the moment and the obstacle in front of her.

✅ Use it when the rules are changing faster than your playbook.

📣 Coaching Leadership

Oprah Winfrey, Host and Television Producer
↳ Develops people through deep questions and long-term investment.

✅ Use it to build a team that can handle disruption.

🌟 Charismatic Leadership

Julia Stewart, Former CEO of IHOP and DineEquity
↳ Moves people through presence, story, and conviction.

✅ Use it to motivate the team and create deep buy-in.

🙌 Authentic Leadership

Michelle Obama, Former First Lady of the US
↳ Leads from her actual values and personality. She doesn't copy!

✅ Use it to build trust internally and externally.

💡 Visionary Leadership

Melanie Perkins, Co-founder and CEO of Canva
↳ Paints the future so clearly the industry plays catch-up.

✅ Use it when building something new.

📃 Values-Led Leadership

Daniela Amodei, President of Anthropic
↳ Makes decisions through the lens of what's right, not just what's easy.

✅ Use it when the right call defines who you are long term.

🎯 Mission-Led Leadership

Jessica Alba, Founder of The Honest Company
↳ Builds the company around a non-negotiable mission and refuses to compromise.

✅ Use it when you need to rally the team around one goal.

🫴 Delegative Leadership

Reese Witherspoon, Founder of Hello Sunshine
↳ Hires brilliance, trusts the team to deliver, stays out of their way.

✅ Use it with experienced operators who handle autonomy well.

🤲 Servant Leadership

Mira Murati, Founder of Thinking Machines Lab
↳ Removes barriers, prioritises the team's work, leads from behind.

✅ Use it when building long-term loyalty and team strength.

Leaders go wrong when they try to pick one style, usually the one that got them promoted, and apply it to everything.

But a coaching leader can't keep coaching when the situation calls for a fast, hard decision, for example.

When the CEO Keeps Learning, Everyone Grows. Professional development starts with your plan!

I spend most of my week with senior leaders in nonprofits of every size, working on org design, strategy, and leadership development. These are talented, committed people with real vision.

They’re also generous. They ask me to find coaching for a team member who’s struggling, to train their managers how to supervise, or to help their teams feel safe speaking up.

Here’s the opportunity I love to name for them: what about you?

Leadership is not about telling people what you want done. It’s about setting a vision that makes sense for the community you aim to uplift, and doing it with accountability and compassion.

After all, ambition and vision are only as good as your team’s buy-in. Aspiration is only meaningful when it is achievable. And caring about your team is only effective when you know how to hold yourself accountable for your own leadership.

Investing in training for mid-level managers to drive outcomes, build culture, and create pathways to growth is admirable. However, It works best when leaders at the top reflect on their own leadership practice first.

When the person at the very top keeps learning, the whole organization rises.
✨ A CEO who invests in their own learning gives everyone permission to grow.
✨ A CEO who learns to supervise well sets the standard for every manager in the building.
✨ A CEO who makes it safe to speak up, ask questions, and admit mistakes hears the truth, and makes better decisions because of it.
✨ A CEO who truly understands collaborative leadership builds a team that owns the vision together. Vision can start with one person, but it lives with those executing it.

Alongside your plans to develop your team, add one more name to the list: yours.

The best leader I ever knew taught me two things as I was growing and learning:
“Ego, get behind me.”
And "surround yourself with people who are smarter than you."

It’s the best advice I ever received, and I use it to this day in all of my work.

DAY 20/30 | YOU DON'T HAVE TO HAVE IT ALL FIGURED OUT TO BEGIN.

I have come to realise that some of the things we are most passionate about are also the things that frighten us the most. Not because we don't believe in them, but because we understand the responsibility that comes with bringing them to life. Sometimes, an idea feels safe while it is still in your heart. 

The moment you put it on paper and begin telling people about it, it becomes real, and suddenly the questions begin. Where will the resources come from? Who will believe in it? What if it doesn't work?

But leadership has taught me that clarity doesn't always come before action. Sometimes, it comes through action. You begin with what you know, remain open to learning, invite others to contribute and allow the vision to take shape. You don't need to pretend to have all the answers. You simply need enough conviction to take the next responsible step.

So, if there is something meaningful you have been postponing because you don't feel completely ready, perhaps it is time to begin. Write the idea down. Have the conversation. Ask for help. Take one practical step. You may not have everything you need to finish, but you might already have enough to start.

In 2006, Phanindra Sama, then around 25, wanted to get home for Diwali. Booking a bus ticket was frustrating, no central place to compare operators, check seats, or pay easily. Instead of just accepting it, he started building a solution. That idea became 𝙍𝙚𝙙𝘽𝙪𝙨, now one of India's best-known online bus booking platforms.

Three lessons from the story:

1. 𝐘𝐨𝐮𝐫 𝐩𝐞𝐫𝐬𝐨𝐧𝐚𝐥 𝐟𝐫𝐮𝐬𝐭𝐫𝐚𝐭𝐢𝐨𝐧 𝐜𝐚𝐧 𝐛𝐞 𝐚 𝐛𝐮𝐬𝐢𝐧𝐞𝐬𝐬 𝐢𝐝𝐞𝐚. Many successful startups begin with a problem the founder faced firsthand. If you keep running into the same friction, someone else probably is too.
2. 𝐒𝐭𝐚𝐫𝐭 𝐬𝐦𝐚𝐥𝐥 𝐚𝐧𝐝 𝐯𝐚𝐥𝐢𝐝𝐚𝐭𝐞 𝐞𝐚𝐫𝐥𝐲. RedBus didn't need a huge budget to begin. It needed a clear problem, a simple product, and enough users to prove the idea worked.

FROM CREATIVITY TO INNOVATION: WHAT DOES IT TAKE TO BRING AN IDEA TO MARKET?

On October 22, 2026, I attended the launch of 84X – Unlocking the Path to Market by Van Lang University  and B71. The panel, moderated by Ms. Kylie Lê, left me with six lessons.

1. Innovation starts with a problem, not necessarily a breakthrough idea.

Mr. Vinnie Lauria used Netflix and Blockbuster to show that a more convenient business model can matter more than complex technology.

Looking back at my studies, I often start a project by asking "what product should we make?" and leave the customer for later. Next time, I want to understand who has the problem first.

2. Investors evaluate the people, not only the idea.

As Founding Partner at Golden Gate Ventures, Vinnie looks for:

	•	Vision & Leadership: Can the founder lead a team?
	•	Execution: What have they done, learned, and adjusted?
	•	Scalability: Can the model grow, including internationally?

For students, execution can start small: one talk with a real customer, one simple test, one revision after feedback.

3. Innovation needs a supportive ecosystem.

Mr. Nguyen Duy Vu (CEO, Hanovation) named three resources: education, access to resources, and community support.

It made me rethink networking. Connecting with the right people for the right problem matters more than knowing many people.

4. Triple Helix: Government × Universities × Industry.

Mr. JSERN KHOR stressed clear roles for each party, while Mr. Nguyen Duy Vu suggested bringing real market problems closer to startups. Collaboration creates value when resources are actually connected, not when many organizations simply sign on.

5. Innovation isn't only for people in tech.

Ms. Tuyet Vu  (Managing Partner, Spark Ventures Studio) spoke about the creative economy: design, customer experience, content, and consumer insight.

I used to think innovation had to mean AI or high tech. Now I see that our advantage as students may lie in noticing changes around us and turning them into value.

6. An innovation ecosystem works like a football team.

Jsern (Executive Director, Global Innovation & Impact Center, VLU) compared stakeholders to players in different positions with one goal. If everyone wants to score, who defends?

His question stayed with me: "Who is going to do what and by when?"

It reminded me of group projects in class, where a good plan falls apart when nobody owns a task or a deadline. I want to start every project with that question.

⸻

As a final-year student, I don't want startup knowledge to stay inside presentations and exams. I want to test it in the real world: talk to real people, run small experiments, and fix what doesn't work.

Thank you to the organizers and speakers for such practical perspectives.

Social media is dead...

And that's excellent news if you practice B2B Marketing or if you are simply trying to build your personal brand on LinkedIn. 

In very simple terms, we've gone through three macro phases of social media: 

1.) The golden era of social media (2006 - 2016): Driven by pure network effects with chronological timelines and feeds filled with updates of our connections. 

2.) The Broadcast Media Age (2017 – 2024): A transition phase where feeds started getting separated from connections and where the name of the game was to build a huge following and then broadcast to them (the Kim Kardashian model...) 

3.) The Interest Media Era (2025+): Our feeds are now driven purely by interest and networks or followers mean far less now than they used to. 

In this article I explain why this is GREAT news. Someone with 500 followers and a good content strategy can have the same impact as someone with 50 000 followers. 

It's the best time to get your B2B marketing message out on LinkedIn or to use LinkedIn as a tool to build your personal brand. 

Read on and I'd be keen to hear your thoughts!

Snap Inc. | Director, Americas Marketing

$2.5 billion. That’s the advertising revenue sitting behind this marketing job. Now you have my attention.

Graymatter Executive Opportunity Review

Graymatter isn't affiliated with Snap or this role. We review opportunities because your time is too valuable to waste pursuing the wrong ones.

Graymatter Score: Clarity A | Executive Appeal A- | Role Design A-

What This Job Really Is

This is B2B marketing with a very visible scoreboard. You'll lead Snapchat's vertical marketing strategy across the US and Canada, including 15 major industries representing $2.5B in annual advertising revenue. The job is to make Snapchat more relevant and more valuable to advertisers. That means partnering directly with Sales, understanding what advertisers need, and turning Snapchat's audience, products and cultural relevance into reasons for brands to spend more. You'll oversee industry marketing, thought leadership, research, customer stories, partnerships, events and executive experiences.
And Snap explicitly wants marketing measured against advertiser consideration, qualified engagement, account coverage, revenue influence and ROI. I like that.

You'll Probably Love This If...

You enjoy the intersection of marketing, media and commercial growth.
This isn't corporate brand stewardship. You'll work directly with Sales leadership and major advertisers while tailoring strategies across industries with very different business needs. Retail doesn't buy like CPG. Auto doesn't buy like entertainment. Financial services doesn't buy like fashion. That's the challenge.

This Probably Isn't Your Role If...

You prefer consumer marketing. The customer here is the advertiser. You'll need to understand agencies, media buyers, CMOs and commercial decision-makers as deeply as you understand Snapchat users. You'll also need to be comfortable in a serious matrix across Sales, Product Marketing, Brand, Creative, Research, Marketing Science and global teams.

Before You Apply

1. How large is the Americas Vertical Marketing team?

2. What budget does this Director control?

3. How directly is marketing credited for advertiser revenue growth?

4. Which of the 15 verticals have the biggest upside or biggest problem?

5. And when Sales and Marketing disagree on where investment should go, who decides? And no it can't be rock. paper. scissors. 

6. Snap also expects employees in-office 4+ days per week.

7. The NYC base range of $276K–$414K plus RSUs is strong and reflects the commercial importance of the seat.

The Graymatter Take

This is one of those roles where Marketing gets very close to the money. The mandate isn't simply to make Snapchat look interesting to advertisers. It's to influence billions of dollars in advertising decisions. That's a very different job. Clear market. Clear customer. Clear commercial objective. And unusually clear measurement. Strong role.

Good Luck!

Deloitte recently published a report on one of the most important topics fintech leaders need to think about when considering implementing AI in their product: Trust
 
Why Trust Is So Important
No matter how good your product is, or how market leading your AI agents are, if you don’t have your user’s trust, they won’t use them. This is true for most products, but even more for money. People have worked incredibly hard for their money and they aren’t about to let you lose it for them
 
Key Themes From The Report
There are various dimensions to the lack of trust in AI (within finance):

1️⃣ Data Sharing Concerns: 72% are concerned about sharing financial information with AI
 
2️⃣ Low Recommendation Trust: only 46% trust the accuracy of AI banking recommendations
 
3️⃣ Financial Action Anxiety: 83% are anxious about AI agents taking financial actions without approving each one
 
But, there are also things people like about AI
4️⃣ Time Savings & Utility: 58% say AI saves time compared to traditional research. 53% say AI gives more useful information than traditional search engines. And 43% say it gives better information than bank websites or apps
 
What This Means for Fintechs and What They Can Do
The good news for fintechs is that trust is not a newly important variable. AI just adds a new dimension as fewer people truly understand how it works. And the bigger the knowledge gap the more care is required:

▷ Uncertainty Aversion: tell people exactly how the AI uses their financial and personal data, and how you are protecting them from any bad outcomes
 
▷ Salience & Transparency: don’t hide anything from users, tell them everything they would want to know. And do it without technical language so they can actually engage with the information
 
▷ Reactance: let people change how much information AI can access and what it’s capable of doing. Give users control
 
Key Takeaways
The value and opportunities for AI are huge, and even customers who are worried about it can admit it. And this puts financial companies in a strong position. Because whether users trust their AI is dependant on their own handling of the communication and user journey
 
If fintechs implement the right communication, framing, and build the right user journeys around it, they can gain users’ trust and increase utilisation

Innovation, FinTech, new players.

Last Thursday at 1871’s FinTech Innovation Summit, the Chicago Fed showed a slide mapping the technology vendors behind the largest US clearinghouses. There were thousands of them, and a lot of the banks and clearing firms rely on the same few providers.

The same day, I was in a private Corporate Innovation session on that exact topic. Partway through, most of the people in the room stopped receiving email, because they all use Microsoft and it had just gone down.

The outage ended up lasting two days and reached 74 countries. Courts, banks and government offices were disrupted, and some firms reportedly went back to fax machines to confirm trades.

I don’t think the answer is to stop standardizing on good tools, since that’s usually what makes operations cheaper and faster. But it does mean that when one of those tools fails, it takes a lot down with it, and most teams haven’t thought much about what they’d do in that moment.

A few questions I’d ask any operations team this week: 
- Which single vendor, if it went dark for 24 hours, would stop revenue? 
- Does anyone know the manual fallback, and has anyone actually practiced it? 
- And is that dependency written down anywhere, or just assumed?

The Fed’s framing for the day was “connect and protect,” and I came away thinking most of us have put far more effort into the first part than the second.
